name: Introduction to Computers
description: Hardware, memory, operating systems, networks, web and databases.

questions.text: Which CPU component performs integer arithmetic and bitwise operations?
questions.correct: Arithmetic logic unit (ALU)
questions.explanation: The ALU executes integer arithmetic and logic on operands.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a CPU cache?
questions.correct: Reduce average memory access latency
questions.explanation: Cache stores frequently used instructions and data close to the CPU.

questions.text: Why can a higher clock speed fail to yield better performance than a slower CPU?
questions.correct: Instructions per cycle and workload characteristics differ
questions.wrong2: All CPUs execute one instruction per clock
questions.wrong3: CPU architecture does not affect performance
questions.explanation: Performance also depends on IPC, memory hierarchy and parallelism.

questions.text: Which register normally contains the address of the next instruction?
questions.correct: Program counter
questions.explanation: The program counter identifies the next instruction to fetch.

questions.text: What mainly distinguishes pipelining from parallel cores?
questions.correct: Pipelining overlaps stages of different instructions within a core
questions.wrong2: Pipelining gives every thread its own physical processor
questions.explanation: Instruction pipelines overlap execution stages; cores offer separate execution resources.

questions.text: Which component translates virtual memory addresses to physical addresses?
questions.correct: Memory management unit
questions.explanation: The MMU performs address translation, often using TLB caches.

questions.text: What does a TLB miss usually require?
questions.correct: A page-table lookup
questions.explanation: The translation lookaside buffer caches virtual-to-physical mappings.

questions.text: Which interface is commonly used for modern NVMe SSDs?
questions.correct: PCI Express
questions.explanation: NVMe SSDs commonly communicate over PCIe.

questions.text: Why are SSD random reads typically faster than hard disk random reads?
questions.correct: SSDs have no mechanical seek or rotational delay
questions.wrong1: SSDs always use a larger file system
questions.wrong2: Hard disks do not support caches
questions.explanation: Flash storage avoids disk-head movement and platter rotation.

questions.text: Which bus carries a physical memory location between processor and memory subsystem?
questions.correct: Address bus
questions.explanation: The address bus identifies memory locations involved in a transfer.

questions.text: Which CPU feature supports executing multiple hardware threads on one core?
questions.correct: Simultaneous multithreading
questions.explanation: SMT exposes multiple logical hardware threads on one physical core.

questions.text: What is the likely effect of a branch misprediction in a deep CPU pipeline?
questions.correct: Incorrectly speculated instructions are discarded
questions.wrong1: The operating system deletes the branch
questions.explanation: Branch mispredictions flush or redirect speculative pipeline work.

questions.text: Which is an example of an input device?
questions.correct: Barcode scanner
questions.explanation: A scanner captures external information for the computer.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a UPS?
questions.correct: Provide temporary power and protect against interruptions
questions.explanation: A UPS supplies backup power and commonly conditions incoming power.

questions.text: Why can adding CPU cores fail to linearly accelerate a program?
questions.correct: Sequential work and synchronization limit parallel speedup
questions.wrong1: All software automatically uses every core
questions.wrong2: RAM cannot be used with multiple cores
questions.wrong3: CPU caches stop working with more cores
questions.explanation: Amdahl's law bounds speedup when part of a workload is sequential.

questions.text: Which memory loses its stored data when power is removed?
questions.correct: DRAM
questions.explanation: DRAM is volatile and must be refreshed while powered.

questions.text: Why does a DRAM module require periodic refresh?
questions.correct: Stored capacitor charge leaks over time
questions.wrong2: Addresses are stored only as magnetic fields
questions.wrong3: The processor erases cells after each read
questions.explanation: DRAM encodes bits as tiny electric charges that decay.

questions.text: What distinguishes RAM capacity from memory bandwidth?
questions.correct: Capacity is storage size; bandwidth is transfer rate
questions.wrong1: Both always mean the same thing
questions.wrong2: Bandwidth is measured only in bytes stored
questions.explanation: Memory capacity uses byte units; bandwidth measures bytes transferred per second.

questions.text: What does ECC memory primarily detect or correct?
questions.correct: Certain accidental bit errors
questions.explanation: ECC adds redundant error-correcting information to memory words.

questions.text: Why can swapping cause severe slowdown?
questions.correct: Disk-backed pages have much higher access latency than RAM
questions.explanation: Frequent page-ins and page-outs incur slow storage operations.

questions.text: Which storage retains data without electrical power?
questions.correct: NAND flash
questions.explanation: Flash is nonvolatile storage used by SSDs.

questions.text: Which address-space concept allows distinct processes to use the same virtual address safely?
questions.correct: Independent virtual address mappings
questions.explanation: Per-process page tables can map the same virtual address to different physical pages.

questions.text: What does the term 'page fault' mean?
questions.correct: A referenced virtual page needs operating-system handling
questions.wrong2: A printer used the wrong paper
questions.wrong3: A disk has no free sectors
questions.explanation: A fault can arise from a missing mapping or an access violation.

questions.text: What is copy-on-write memory commonly used for?
questions.correct: Sharing pages until a process modifies one
questions.wrong2: Writing all pages to disk at every instruction
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write delays duplication until a write requires separation.

questions.text: Which is generally the smallest and fastest memory closest to CPU execution units?
questions.correct: CPU register
questions.explanation: Registers are directly accessible by instructions and very low latency.

questions.text: What is a cache hit?
questions.correct: Requested data is already in the cache
questions.wrong1: Data must be retrieved from remote disk
questions.wrong2: Memory has run out of address space
questions.explanation: A hit avoids fetching the requested block from a lower memory level.

questions.text: What does the write-back cache policy do?
questions.correct: Defers lower-level writes until a modified line is evicted
questions.wrong1: Writes every store immediately to all media
questions.explanation: Write-back caches mark dirty lines and later propagate updates.

questions.text: What is the major purpose of a file system?
questions.correct: Organize and track files and directories on storage
questions.explanation: File systems manage names, metadata and mapping of data to blocks.

questions.text: Why does fragmentation most affect a mechanical disk's sequential file read?
questions.correct: Dispersed extents require more head movement
questions.wrong1: Fragmentation changes the CPU's instruction set
questions.wrong3: It converts files into encrypted data
questions.explanation: Noncontiguous extents increase seek overhead on spinning media.

questions.text: What does RAID 1 provide?
questions.correct: Mirrored copies of data across drives
questions.wrong2: Parity across at least three disks only
questions.explanation: RAID 1 mirrors data, increasing resilience against a single drive failure.

questions.text: Why is RAID not a replacement for a backup?
questions.correct: It cannot reliably recover deleted or corrupted data replicated to all drives
questions.wrong2: RAID always stores an off-site copy
questions.wrong3: RAID eliminates the need for restore tests
questions.explanation: Redundancy helps with drive failure but not deletion or many logical disasters.

questions.text: Which unit equals 1024 mebibytes?
questions.correct: One gibibyte (GiB)
questions.explanation: Binary prefixes define 1 GiB as 1024 MiB.

questions.text: What is the maximum addressable memory using 32-bit byte addresses without extensions?
questions.correct: 4 GiB
questions.explanation: Two to the power 32 byte addresses give 4 GiB of address space.

questions.text: Which technology commonly enables automatic SSD wear leveling?
questions.correct: Flash translation layer
questions.explanation: The FTL remaps logical addresses to distribute flash erase cycles.

questions.text: What does a process represent?
questions.correct: A program instance with its own execution context
questions.explanation: A process is an executing program with managed resources.

questions.text: How does a thread usually differ from a separate process?
questions.correct: Threads in a process share its address space
questions.wrong1: Threads always have separate physical RAM
questions.wrong3: Threads do not have a call stack
questions.explanation: Threads share process memory while maintaining their own execution state.

questions.text: What is a context switch?
questions.correct: Saving one task's state and restoring another's
questions.explanation: Schedulers switch CPU execution between tasks using context state.

questions.text: What is a necessary condition for deadlock?
questions.correct: A circular wait among held and requested resources
questions.wrong2: Every thread must release resources instantly
questions.wrong3: No task may hold a lock
questions.explanation: Circular wait is one of the Coffman deadlock conditions.

questions.text: What is a race condition?
questions.correct: Output depends on timing of concurrent operations
questions.wrong1: A network cable runs faster than another
questions.wrong2: An error caused only by thermal throttling
questions.wrong3: A database table has no primary key
questions.explanation: A race arises when unsynchronized interleavings affect results.

questions.text: Which tool directly controls concurrent access to a critical section?
questions.correct: Mutex
questions.explanation: A mutex ensures exclusive ownership of a protected critical section.

questions.text: What is a system call?
questions.correct: A controlled request from user code to the operating-system kernel
questions.wrong1: An instruction to send email automatically
questions.wrong2: A command only for BIOS setup
questions.wrong3: A call between unrelated network routers
questions.explanation: System calls provide controlled access to privileged OS services.

questions.text: Why does virtual memory improve process isolation?
questions.correct: Different processes receive controlled virtual address spaces
questions.wrong1: All applications share the same writable page table
questions.explanation: Page tables and protection bits prevent unauthorized address-space access.

questions.text: What is the role of a device driver?
questions.correct: Translate OS requests into device-specific operations
questions.explanation: Drivers interface operating systems with hardware devices.

questions.text: What does preemptive scheduling permit?
questions.correct: The OS interrupts a running task to schedule another
questions.wrong1: Tasks yield only when they explicitly choose
questions.wrong2: All tasks share a single stack
questions.explanation: Preemptive kernels can reclaim CPU time using timer interrupts.

questions.text: Which filesystem permission lets a Unix user execute a file?
questions.correct: x bit
questions.explanation: The execute bit authorizes execution or traversal for directories.

questions.text: Why can a zombie process exist in Unix-like systems?
questions.correct: Its parent has not yet collected its exit status
questions.wrong3: The kernel lost the process binary
questions.explanation: Exited processes may retain minimal process-table metadata until reaped.

questions.text: What does kernel mode permit that user mode ordinarily does not?
questions.correct: Execution of privileged instructions
questions.wrong3: Direct editing of CPU microcode by JavaScript
questions.explanation: Kernel privilege enables protected hardware operations.

questions.text: What does starvation mean in scheduling?
questions.correct: A runnable task waits indefinitely for needed service
questions.wrong1: A task uses no RAM at all
questions.wrong3: A device runs on battery power
questions.explanation: Unfair resource allocation can indefinitely postpone a task.

questions.text: Which mechanism prevents arbitrary user programs writing kernel memory?
questions.correct: Memory protection enforced by CPU and OS
questions.explanation: Privilege and page protections restrict memory writes.

questions.text: Why is a journaling file system useful after a crash?
questions.correct: It logs metadata changes to aid consistency recovery
questions.wrong1: It guarantees zero lost application bytes
questions.wrong2: It removes the need for backups
questions.wrong3: It encrypts all files by default
questions.explanation: Journaling helps replay or roll back incomplete file-system operations.

questions.text: What does a container normally share with its host?
questions.correct: Operating-system kernel
questions.explanation: Containers isolate processes while typically sharing the host kernel.

questions.text: What does a hypervisor primarily provide?
questions.correct: Isolation and management of virtual machines
questions.explanation: Hypervisors virtualize hardware resources for guest operating systems.

questions.text: Which mechanism limits a process's accessible system resources in Linux containers?
questions.correct: cgroups
questions.explanation: Linux control groups account for and limit resource consumption.

questions.text: Why can a 64-bit OS run out of usable RAM before its virtual addresses are exhausted?
questions.correct: Physical memory and resource limits are much smaller than virtual address space
questions.wrong1: Virtual addresses are always physical slots
questions.wrong2: All 64-bit CPUs require 64 exabytes of installed RAM
questions.wrong3: Virtual memory works only on SSDs
questions.explanation: Virtual addresses provide a large mapping space; RAM capacity remains finite.

questions.text: What is the primary job of a router?
questions.correct: Forward packets between IP networks
questions.explanation: Routers choose paths and forward network-layer traffic.

questions.text: Why is a switch's MAC table useful?
questions.correct: It maps learned MAC addresses to switch ports for targeted forwarding
questions.wrong3: It converts IPv6 packets into HTML
questions.explanation: Switches learn source MAC addresses and select outgoing ports.

questions.text: Which OSI layer is associated with IP routing?
questions.correct: Network layer (Layer 3)
questions.explanation: IP is a network-layer addressing and forwarding protocol.

questions.text: How many usable host addresses does a conventional IPv4 /27 subnet provide?
questions.explanation: A /27 has 32 total addresses; network and broadcast are not host addresses.

questions.text: Which protocol dynamically assigns IPv4 addresses on many local networks?
questions.correct: DHCP
questions.explanation: DHCP supplies addresses and other network configuration.

questions.text: What happens when DNS resolution succeeds but TCP connection fails?
questions.correct: The name resolves but the target service may be unreachable
questions.wrong1: DNS automatically proves the web server is healthy
questions.wrong3: The browser must format its cache
questions.explanation: DNS lookup and transport connectivity are independent stages.

questions.text: What is a common secure port for HTTPS over TCP?
questions.explanation: HTTPS commonly uses TCP port 443, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP 443.

questions.text: Which TCP mechanism helps avoid overwhelming a receiver?
questions.correct: Flow control using the advertised receive window
questions.explanation: TCP's receive window limits unacknowledged data to receiver capacity.

questions.text: What does TCP provide that plain UDP does not provide by default?
questions.correct: Ordered reliable byte-stream delivery
questions.explanation: TCP retransmits lost segments and orders the delivered byte stream.

questions.text: Why can two machines on the same LAN use the same private IPv4 address only with special isolation?
questions.correct: Address conflict disrupts normal local delivery
questions.wrong1: All routers always assign duplicate addresses
questions.explanation: Duplicate addresses on a shared broadcast domain cause ARP and routing ambiguity.

questions.text: What is the role of ARP in IPv4 Ethernet networks?
questions.correct: Resolve local IPv4 addresses to link-layer MAC addresses
questions.explanation: ARP maps a local IPv4 next-hop address to an Ethernet MAC address.

questions.text: What does a /24 IPv4 CIDR prefix specify?
questions.correct: The first 24 address bits are the network prefix
questions.explanation: CIDR prefixes denote the number of fixed network bits.

questions.text: What is NAT commonly used for on home routers?
questions.correct: Translate private addresses and ports to public-facing mappings
questions.explanation: NAT often lets many private hosts share a public IPv4 address.

questions.text: Why does HTTP/3 use QUIC instead of TCP as its transport?
questions.correct: QUIC supports encrypted multiplexed streams over UDP
questions.wrong1: UDP guarantees ordered delivery without a protocol
questions.wrong2: HTTP/3 removes the need for TLS
questions.explanation: QUIC integrates reliable stream handling and TLS over UDP.

questions.text: Which record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address?
questions.correct: DNS A record
questions.explanation: A records hold IPv4 addresses; AAAA records hold IPv6 addresses.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a TCP three-way handshake?
questions.correct: Establish connection state and synchronize initial sequence numbers
questions.explanation: SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK establish initial transport state.

questions.text: Which device separates collision domains per Ethernet port?
questions.correct: Network switch
questions.explanation: Each switched Ethernet port forms its own collision domain.

questions.text: What can cause packet loss even when links are physically healthy?
questions.correct: Congestion and full router queues
questions.explanation: Network buffers can overflow under load.

questions.text: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
questions.explanation: IPv6 uses ::1 for the loopback interface.

questions.text: Which statement about a VLAN is correct?
questions.correct: It creates a logical Layer 2 broadcast domain
questions.wrong2: It is identical to a WAN
questions.wrong3: It removes the need for IP addressing
questions.explanation: VLAN tags segment switch traffic into distinct Layer 2 domains.

questions.text: What does the ping utility generally test?
questions.correct: ICMP echo reachability and latency
questions.explanation: Ping exchanges ICMP echo messages and measures round-trip times.

questions.text: Why is an MTU mismatch a possible cause of connection problems?
questions.correct: Oversized packets may be dropped if fragmentation or discovery fails
questions.wrong1: MTU changes the CPU word length
questions.wrong2: MTU controls the number of DNS zones
questions.explanation: Path MTU issues can prevent delivery of packets that exceed link limits.

questions.text: What is the role of a default gateway?
questions.correct: Forward traffic destined outside the local subnet
questions.explanation: Hosts send off-subnet packets toward a configured next-hop router.

questions.text: Which wireless security generation requires protected management frames for all certified personal-mode connections?
questions.correct: WPA3
questions.explanation: WPA3 mandates protected management frames in certified WPA3 deployments.

questions.text: Which protocol is commonly used to synchronize system clocks over IP networks?
questions.correct: NTP
questions.explanation: Network Time Protocol synchronizes clocks using time sources.

questions.text: What best describes round-trip time (RTT)?
questions.correct: Time for a message to reach a destination and for its response to return
questions.wrong1: Size of the largest Ethernet frame
questions.wrong2: Number of hops in a route only
questions.explanation: RTT includes forward and reverse paths plus processing delays.

questions.text: What does HTTP status 404 indicate?
questions.correct: Requested resource was not found
questions.wrong1: The request succeeded and returned content
questions.explanation: HTTP 404 means the target resource was not found.

questions.text: Why can an HTTP GET be retried safely more often than a typical POST?
questions.correct: GET is defined as safe/idempotent while POST may cause state changes
questions.wrong1: GET always uses TLS and POST never does
questions.wrong2: GET bodies must contain SQL queries
questions.explanation: HTTP method semantics guide automatic retry behavior.

questions.text: What does a browser cookie commonly provide?
questions.correct: Client-side storage of small state identifiers
questions.explanation: Cookies can carry session identifiers or small preferences.

questions.text: What is the Same-Origin Policy intended to restrict?
questions.correct: Cross-origin scripts reading protected resources without permission
questions.explanation: Browser origins isolate access to sensitive cross-origin resources.

questions.text: Which part of a URL normally identifies the domain host?
questions.correct: Hostname
questions.explanation: The host portion identifies the server name or address.

questions.text: What is a CDN's primary performance advantage for geographically dispersed users?
questions.correct: Serve cached content from nearby edge locations
questions.wrong3: Compile source code in the browser
questions.explanation: Edge caching can reduce network distance and origin load.

questions.text: What is TLS primarily used to provide?
questions.correct: Authenticated encrypted communication channels
questions.explanation: TLS protects data in transit and can authenticate the server.

questions.text: Why can an HTTPS page still contain untrusted content?
questions.correct: TLS protects transport, not the truthfulness of page content
questions.wrong3: Certificates guarantee the site owner's ethics
questions.explanation: Transport encryption does not certify that application content is trustworthy.

questions.text: What does a web server return with an HTTP 301 status?
questions.correct: Permanent redirect
questions.explanation: 301 indicates that the requested resource moved permanently.

questions.text: Which browser storage normally persists across tabs and restarts for one origin?
questions.correct: localStorage
questions.explanation: localStorage persists until it is explicitly cleared or removed.

questions.text: What does an API endpoint normally represent?
questions.correct: An address exposing an application operation or resource
questions.explanation: An endpoint specifies an API location clients interact with.

questions.text: Why is HTTP 429 different from HTTP 503?
questions.correct: 429 indicates rate limiting; 503 indicates temporary service unavailability
questions.explanation: Different status codes distinguish client request-rate limits from server availability.

questions.text: Which status code commonly means a client lacks valid authentication credentials?
questions.explanation: HTTP 401 signals missing or invalid authentication credentials.

questions.text: Which HTTP response header helps stop MIME type sniffing?
questions.correct: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
questions.explanation: The nosniff directive tells browsers to honor declared content types.

questions.text: What is a reverse proxy commonly used for?
questions.correct: Route client requests to backend services
questions.explanation: Reverse proxies can terminate TLS and distribute traffic among services.

questions.text: Why should a backend validate input even when the frontend already validates it?
questions.correct: Clients can bypass browser-side validation
questions.explanation: Only server-side enforcement can reliably protect trust boundaries.

questions.text: What is WebSocket mainly designed for?
questions.correct: Persistent bidirectional communication
questions.explanation: WebSocket provides a persistent two-way channel after handshake.

questions.text: Which browser event indicates a background tab may no longer receive the same timer cadence?
questions.correct: visibilitychange
questions.explanation: Browsers may throttle background tabs; visibilitychange reports document visibility.

questions.text: What is DNS caching intended to reduce?
questions.correct: Repeated resolver queries and lookup latency
questions.explanation: Cached DNS answers can avoid repeated remote resolution.

questions.text: Why is a service worker not a substitute for a backend authorization check?
questions.correct: Service workers execute under client control and cannot enforce server trust
questions.wrong1: Service workers can decrypt all server data
questions.wrong2: Service workers run with database administrator privilege
questions.explanation: Authorization must be checked on the server for each protected resource.

questions.text: What is the binary representation of decimal 13?
questions.explanation: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, giving binary 1101.

questions.text: How many distinct values can an unsigned 10-bit field represent?
questions.explanation: An unsigned n-bit field represents 2 to the power n distinct patterns.

questions.text: What does a primary key enforce in a relational table?
questions.correct: Unique identification of rows
questions.wrong3: A permanent connection to the internet
questions.explanation: Primary key constraints prevent null and duplicate key values.

questions.text: Why can indexing speed up selective queries but slow writes?
questions.correct: Indexes require maintenance when data changes
questions.wrong2: All indexes keep data only in CPU registers
questions.explanation: Indexes trade extra storage and update work for faster lookups.

questions.text: What does a foreign key normally enforce?
questions.correct: Referential integrity between related tables
questions.explanation: Foreign keys constrain references to permitted parent keys.

questions.text: Which transaction property prevents partially applied changes from becoming permanent?
questions.correct: Atomicity
questions.explanation: Atomic transactions commit all changes or none.

questions.text: What is database normalization mainly intended to reduce?
questions.correct: Data redundancy and modification anomalies
questions.explanation: Normalization separates data based on functional dependencies.

questions.text: What problem can occur with a non-repeatable read under weak isolation?
questions.correct: The same row returns different committed values within one transaction
questions.wrong1: The table loses all rows automatically
questions.explanation: A concurrent transaction may update a row between reads.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of the SQL GROUP BY clause?
questions.correct: Group records for aggregate calculation
questions.explanation: GROUP BY forms groups to calculate aggregates such as counts or sums.

questions.text: What does the SQL HAVING clause usually filter?
questions.correct: Groups after aggregation
questions.explanation: HAVING applies conditions to grouped aggregate results.

questions.text: What does ACID refer to?
questions.correct: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
questions.explanation: ACID describes core transaction guarantees.

questions.text: Why can a deadlock occur between two database transactions?
questions.correct: They hold locks while waiting for each other's locked resources
questions.wrong1: Every SQL SELECT implicitly deletes records
questions.wrong2: All tables use the same timestamp
questions.explanation: Circular lock dependencies create deadlock until one transaction is aborted.

questions.text: What is the result of binary 1010 AND binary 1100?
questions.explanation: Only the bit set in both operands remains set.

questions.text: What does two's-complement encoding enable in binary arithmetic?
questions.correct: Unified addition for positive and negative integers
questions.explanation: Two's complement represents negative numbers so ordinary binary adders work for signed arithmetic.

questions.text: Why can speculative execution require security mitigations?
questions.correct: Microarchitectural side effects may expose information despite discarded instruction results
questions.wrong1: Speculation disables process isolation by definition
questions.wrong3: All pipelines use the same memory address
questions.explanation: Side channels can leak information from transiently executed instructions.

questions.text: What is the consequence of a memory access violating a page's permissions?
questions.correct: A protection fault or exception
questions.wrong1: Automatic creation of a new user account
questions.explanation: The CPU and operating system enforce page permission bits.

questions.text: What is a key difference between a stateful firewall and a stateless packet filter?
questions.correct: A stateful firewall tracks connection context
questions.wrong1: A stateless filter always encrypts packets
questions.wrong2: A stateful firewall does not inspect any ports
questions.wrong3: Stateless filtering requires a database server
questions.explanation: Connection tracking lets stateful rules treat replies differently from unsolicited traffic.

questions.text: Why does a cache-control private directive matter for authenticated HTTP responses?
questions.correct: It prevents shared intermediary caches from storing user-specific responses
questions.wrong3: It disables the browser's TCP connection
questions.explanation: The private directive restricts caching to a user's own cache rather than shared proxies.

questions.text: What does priority inversion describe?
questions.correct: A high-priority task waits for a lock held by a lower-priority task
questions.wrong3: A program receives a lower process ID
questions.explanation: Locks held by low-priority work can delay higher-priority tasks.

questions.text: How does DMA reduce CPU overhead during large I/O transfers?
questions.correct: A controller transfers data between a device and memory without per-byte CPU copying
questions.wrong1: It bypasses all memory access controls
questions.wrong3: It removes the need for interrupt handling
questions.explanation: Direct memory access moves bulk data while the CPU sets up and coordinates the transfer.

name: Programming
description: C++, Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, algorithms and APIs.

questions.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
questions.correct: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search interval each step.

questions.text: What is the worst-case complexity of appending to a dynamic array when it must resize?
questions.correct: O(n)
questions.explanation: Growing an array may copy all existing elements; amortized append can still be O(1).

questions.text: What data structure follows FIFO order?
questions.correct: Queue
questions.explanation: A queue removes elements in first-in, first-out order.

questions.text: Why is a hash-table lookup not guaranteed O(1) worst case?
questions.correct: Hash collisions may cause many keys to share a bucket
questions.wrong1: Hash tables must sort after every lookup
questions.wrong2: Every key uses a new process
questions.explanation: Collisions can degrade lookup depending on collision strategy.

questions.text: What is the base case of a recursive function?
questions.correct: The condition that stops further recursive calls
questions.wrong3: The only loop in the function
questions.explanation: A recursive algorithm needs a terminating condition.

questions.text: What does stable sorting guarantee?
questions.correct: Equal-key elements preserve their original relative order
questions.explanation: Stable sorts retain the relative order of items with equal keys.

questions.text: Which design principle favors a function having one well-defined responsibility?
questions.correct: Single Responsibility Principle
questions.explanation: Single responsibility reduces unrelated reasons for changing one unit.

questions.text: Why can an algorithm be O(n log n) despite having nested loops?
questions.correct: An inner loop may shrink or operate logarithmically
questions.wrong1: All nested loops are O(n squared)
questions.wrong2: Big-O is determined by programming language
questions.wrong3: Any recursion makes an algorithm O(1)
questions.explanation: Loop bounds and total work determine asymptotic complexity.

questions.text: Which data structure is most suitable for matching nested parentheses?
questions.correct: Stack
questions.explanation: A stack matches closing delimiters with the most recent opening delimiter.

questions.text: What does topological sorting require?
questions.correct: A directed acyclic graph
questions.wrong3: A graph with negative edge weights
questions.explanation: A topological ordering exists for DAGs.

questions.text: What is an invariant in an algorithm?
questions.correct: A property maintained throughout specified execution steps
questions.wrong1: A value that can never be read
questions.explanation: Loop invariants support reasoning about algorithm correctness.

questions.text: Which search algorithm finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs?
questions.correct: Breadth-first search
questions.explanation: BFS explores edges in increasing distance from the start.

questions.text: What does an interface typically specify?
questions.correct: A contract of available operations
questions.wrong1: The exact RAM address of an object
questions.explanation: Interfaces define what operations implementations must support.

questions.text: Why can memoization reduce exponential recursion?
questions.correct: It caches results of repeated subproblems
questions.wrong1: It increases recursion depth without bounds
questions.wrong2: It compiles function calls to assembly text
questions.wrong3: It changes all integers to strings
questions.explanation: Memoization avoids recomputing identical subproblem results.

questions.text: What does immutability mean for a value?
questions.correct: The value cannot be changed after creation
questions.wrong1: The value can never be copied
questions.wrong2: The value is always stored in ROM
questions.wrong3: The value must be globally accessible
questions.explanation: Immutable values are replaced rather than modified in place.

questions.text: How does dependency injection generally improve testability?
questions.correct: It allows replacing dependencies with controlled implementations
questions.explanation: Constructor or parameter injection can substitute mocks or fakes for tests.

questions.text: What property distinguishes a pure function?
questions.correct: Same inputs give same result without observable side effects
questions.wrong1: It must make an HTTP request
questions.wrong2: It may mutate global state freely
questions.wrong3: It always runs in constant time
questions.explanation: Pure functions have referentially transparent behavior.

questions.text: Why does a priority queue normally use a heap?
questions.correct: It offers efficient access and updates for extreme-priority items
questions.wrong1: A heap always stores data in insertion order
questions.explanation: Binary heaps support O(log n) insertion and removal of the top-priority item.

questions.text: What does the C++ keyword const express for an object?
questions.correct: It cannot be modified through that const-qualified access
questions.wrong1: It is always stored in CPU cache
questions.wrong2: It is automatically a global variable
questions.explanation: Const qualification restricts modification through that access path.

questions.text: What does std::move do by itself?
questions.correct: Cast an expression to an rvalue reference category
questions.explanation: std::move enables move-aware operations but does not itself transfer resources.

questions.text: Which standard library container offers contiguous storage and dynamic resizing?
questions.correct: std::vector
questions.explanation: std::vector stores elements contiguously and grows as needed.

questions.text: What is a dangling pointer?
questions.correct: A pointer referring to storage whose lifetime has ended
questions.wrong2: A pointer to a global variable
questions.wrong3: A pointer held in a shared_ptr
questions.explanation: Dereferencing a pointer after object lifetime ends is undefined behavior.

questions.text: Why is RAII useful in C++?
questions.correct: Resource cleanup is tied to object lifetime
questions.wrong1: Every object gets a separate operating system thread
questions.wrong3: It replaces all smart pointers with arrays
questions.explanation: RAII constructors acquire resources and destructors release them.

questions.text: What is the ownership implication of std::unique_ptr?
questions.correct: Exclusive ownership of a dynamically managed object
questions.explanation: A unique_ptr is movable but not copyable and owns its resource exclusively.

questions.text: What is the main role of std::shared_ptr?
questions.correct: Reference-counted shared ownership
questions.explanation: shared_ptr manages shared ownership through a reference count.

questions.text: Why can a cycle of std::shared_ptr objects leak memory?
questions.correct: Reference counts may never fall to zero
questions.wrong1: shared_ptr does not call destructors normally
questions.wrong2: The compiler stores pointers only in registers
questions.wrong3: Any pointer cycle is a compiler error
questions.explanation: Use weak_ptr to break cycles of shared ownership.

questions.text: What does virtual dispatch select?
questions.correct: An override based on the dynamic object type
questions.wrong1: A function solely from source-file name
questions.explanation: Virtual functions support runtime polymorphism.

questions.text: Why should a polymorphic base class commonly have a virtual destructor?
questions.correct: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer must invoke proper destruction
questions.wrong2: It reduces every object to one byte
questions.explanation: Virtual destruction correctly destroys derived resources via a base pointer.

questions.text: Which keyword prevents implicit conversion for many constructors?
questions.correct: explicit
questions.explanation: The explicit specifier restricts implicit constructor-based conversions.

questions.text: What is object slicing?
questions.correct: Copying a derived object into a base value loses its derived portion
questions.wrong1: Converting a reference into a unique_ptr
questions.wrong3: Moving an object between CPU cores
questions.explanation: By-value base copies preserve only the base subobject.

questions.text: What does the scope resolution operator :: do?
questions.correct: Qualify a name with a namespace or class scope
questions.explanation: :: selects names in an explicit scope.

questions.text: When can std::vector iterator invalidation occur?
questions.correct: Reallocation may invalidate all iterators and references
questions.wrong1: Only when a compiler warning appears
questions.explanation: Capacity growth relocates elements and invalidates prior positions.

questions.text: What is a reference in C++?
questions.correct: An alias bound to an existing object or function
questions.wrong2: A string representation of an address
questions.explanation: References are aliases with language-specific binding rules.

questions.text: Which rule applies to modifying the same scalar from unsynchronized C++ threads?
questions.correct: It can constitute a data race and undefined behavior
questions.wrong2: The last thread always wins deterministically
questions.wrong3: It is safe whenever values are small
questions.explanation: Concurrent conflicting accesses without suitable synchronization cause a data race.

questions.text: What is the result of integer division 7 / 2 in C++ when both operands are int?
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero.

questions.text: What does noexcept communicate about a C++ function?
questions.correct: Its declared exception specification forbids exceptions escaping
questions.wrong3: It means the function cannot allocate memory
questions.explanation: Violating a nonthrowing exception specification calls std::terminate.

questions.text: Which header declares std::sort?
questions.correct: <algorithm>
questions.explanation: std::sort is defined in the algorithm standard header.

questions.text: Why does accessing a std::map by operator[] potentially modify it?
questions.correct: It inserts a default-initialized value when the key is absent
questions.wrong1: It sorts the whole map into a vector
questions.explanation: map::operator[] creates an entry if the key does not exist.

questions.text: What does Python's list.append(x) return?
questions.correct: None
questions.explanation: append mutates the list in place and returns None.

questions.text: Why is a mutable default argument in Python risky?
questions.correct: The same object can be reused across calls
questions.wrong1: Python copies all defaults per call
questions.explanation: Default expressions are evaluated when the function is defined.

questions.text: Which Python type is immutable?
questions.correct: tuple
questions.explanation: Tuples cannot be modified in place after creation.

questions.text: What does `a is b` test in Python?
questions.correct: Object identity
questions.explanation: is compares whether references denote the same object.

questions.text: Which expression creates a dictionary comprehension?
questions.correct: {x: x*x for x in range(3)}
questions.explanation: Dictionary comprehensions use key:value expressions within braces.

questions.text: Why does iterating a generator often use less memory than building a list?
questions.correct: Values can be produced lazily
questions.wrong1: Generators always store all results in RAM
questions.wrong2: Generators execute without a Python interpreter
questions.explanation: Generators yield items as needed instead of materializing them together.

questions.text: What does `enumerate(items)` provide?
questions.correct: Index and item pairs
questions.explanation: enumerate yields pairs of sequence index and element.

questions.text: What is the difference between `==` and `is` for two equal but distinct lists?
questions.correct: == can be true while is is false
questions.explanation: Equality compares values while identity compares object references.

questions.text: Which exception is raised for accessing a missing dictionary key with `d[key]`?
questions.correct: KeyError
questions.explanation: Dictionary subscripting raises KeyError when a key is missing.

questions.text: What does the `with` statement usually guarantee for a context manager?
questions.correct: Its exit method executes when leaving the block, including on exceptions
questions.wrong2: It prevents all file I/O errors
questions.wrong3: It creates a new operating system process
questions.explanation: Context manager cleanup occurs through __exit__.

questions.text: What is the result of `len({1,1,2})`?
questions.explanation: A set removes duplicate values, leaving 1 and 2.

questions.text: What does a shallow copy of a nested list retain?
questions.correct: References to the same nested objects
questions.wrong3: A shared reference to the outer list itself
questions.explanation: The outer container is copied but nested elements are shared.

questions.text: Which keyword introduces an asynchronous function in Python?
questions.correct: async def
questions.explanation: Async functions are declared with async def.

questions.text: Why does `asyncio` not automatically accelerate CPU-bound Python code?
questions.correct: Cooperative concurrency does not make CPU work parallel
questions.wrong1: Every coroutine executes on a different CPU core
questions.wrong2: The event loop removes the GIL
questions.explanation: An event loop remains blocked by long CPU-bound work unless it is offloaded.

questions.text: What does the slice `numbers[::-1]` commonly produce?
questions.correct: A reversed copy of the sequence
questions.wrong3: A reference to the original object only
questions.explanation: A step of -1 traverses a sequence backwards.

questions.text: Why can `list.sort()` return None even after successfully sorting?
questions.correct: It sorts the list in place by design
questions.wrong2: It only works on immutable tuples
questions.explanation: sort performs an in-place mutation and returns None.

questions.text: Which operator tests membership in a collection?
questions.correct: in
questions.explanation: The in operator checks whether a value is contained in a collection.

questions.text: What is the major difference between `@staticmethod` and `@classmethod`?
questions.correct: A classmethod receives the class as its first implicit argument
questions.wrong3: Classmethods cannot be called on instances
questions.explanation: classmethod binds cls while staticmethod gets no implicit instance or class.

questions.text: What does `pip` primarily manage?
questions.correct: Python packages
questions.explanation: pip installs and manages Python distributions.

questions.text: What happens when a list is multiplied as `[[]] * 3`?
questions.correct: Three references to the same inner list are produced
questions.wrong1: Three independent inner lists are deep-copied
questions.explanation: Sequence multiplication replicates references to contained objects.

questions.text: What does `===` compare in JavaScript?
questions.correct: Strict equality without type coercion
questions.explanation: Strict equality compares values with compatible types and references for objects.

questions.text: Why does `typeof null` evaluate to `object`?
questions.correct: It is a historical language quirk
questions.explanation: The result is a long-standing JavaScript compatibility behavior.

questions.text: What does `Array.map()` normally return?
questions.correct: A new array of transformed elements
questions.explanation: map constructs an array from callback results.

questions.text: What is the event loop's role in browser JavaScript?
questions.correct: Schedule queued callbacks and microtasks around synchronous execution
questions.wrong1: Execute all JavaScript callbacks on independent OS threads
questions.wrong2: Remove the need for asynchronous APIs
questions.explanation: The event loop processes tasks after the current call stack unwinds.

questions.text: What does `Promise.all` do if one input promise rejects?
questions.correct: Reject the combined promise
questions.explanation: Promise.all rejects when any member rejects.

questions.text: What generally executes before the next timer callback after a resolved Promise?
questions.correct: Queued promise microtasks
questions.explanation: The microtask queue is drained at the relevant microtask checkpoint.

questions.text: What does the `let` keyword provide?
questions.correct: Block-scoped variable binding
questions.explanation: let declares a mutable block-scoped binding.

questions.text: Why can a `const` object still have mutable properties?
questions.correct: const fixes the binding, not the referenced object's internal state
questions.wrong3: Object properties are copied on every read
questions.explanation: Object mutability is independent of whether the variable binding is reassigned.

questions.text: Which method parses JSON text into a JavaScript value?
questions.correct: JSON.parse
questions.explanation: JSON.parse converts valid JSON text to values.

questions.text: Why can `0 == false` be true while `0 === false` is false?
questions.correct: Loose equality coerces types; strict equality does not
questions.wrong1: Strict equality always converts booleans to numbers
questions.explanation: Abstract equality applies coercion between number and boolean.

questions.text: Which API selects the first DOM element matching a CSS selector?
questions.correct: document.querySelector
questions.explanation: querySelector returns the first matched element or null.

questions.text: Why is `innerHTML` dangerous when used with untrusted text?
questions.correct: It can introduce attacker-controlled HTML and script execution paths
questions.wrong1: It performs automatic parameterized SQL queries
questions.explanation: Use textContent for ordinary untrusted text to avoid HTML injection.

questions.text: What does `fetch()` initially resolve with for an HTTP 404 response?
questions.correct: A Response object with ok equal to false
questions.wrong1: A rejected promise solely because status is 404
questions.explanation: fetch resolves on HTTP responses; it rejects on network-level failures.

questions.text: What is an AbortController used for?
questions.correct: Signal cancellation to APIs such as fetch
questions.wrong2: Copy DOM nodes into another process
questions.explanation: An AbortSignal lets cooperating APIs cancel outstanding operations.

questions.text: What is a closure?
questions.correct: A function retaining access to its lexical environment
questions.explanation: Closures capture variables from the surrounding lexical scope.

questions.text: What can make sequential await calls slower than independent Promise.all tasks?
questions.correct: Unnecessary serial waiting for independent operations
questions.wrong3: All async functions execute in separate processes
questions.explanation: Independent requests can overlap rather than wait on each other's completion.

questions.text: What is a JavaScript module export?
questions.correct: A binding made accessible to importing modules
questions.explanation: export exposes named or default module members.

questions.text: What is the main difference between Object.freeze and deep freezing?
questions.correct: Object.freeze protects only an object's own properties at the first level
questions.wrong1: Object.freeze recursively freezes every nested object
questions.wrong2: Deep freezing works only on arrays
questions.explanation: Nested objects remain mutable unless individually frozen.

questions.text: Which HTML element provides a semantic label for a form control?
questions.correct: <label>
questions.explanation: Labels associate text with input controls and improve accessibility.

questions.text: Why should form labels use the correct `for` and `id` pairing?
questions.correct: Activating a label can focus or toggle the associated input
questions.wrong1: It automatically validates an API token
questions.wrong3: It changes the form's HTTP method
questions.explanation: Matching for/id creates a programmatic relationship for accessibility.

questions.text: What does the HTML `alt` attribute describe?
questions.correct: Alternative text for images
questions.explanation: Alternative text communicates meaningful image content when needed.

questions.text: What is the effect of `defer` on an external classic script?
questions.correct: Execute after HTML parsing and before DOMContentLoaded
questions.wrong1: Execute before any HTML is parsed
questions.wrong3: Convert the script into a stylesheet
questions.explanation: Deferred scripts download in parallel and execute after parsing in document order.

questions.text: Which HTML element identifies the main content of a page?
questions.correct: <main>
questions.explanation: The main landmark represents the dominant page content.

questions.text: Why is a button's `type` important inside a form?
questions.correct: The default submit behavior can trigger an unintended form submission
questions.wrong3: HTML cannot submit forms without JavaScript
questions.explanation: A button without an explicit type defaults to submit in a form.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a semantic `<nav>` element?
questions.correct: Identify a section containing navigation links
questions.explanation: nav marks a navigation landmark for users and assistive technology.

questions.text: How does CSS specificity commonly compare ID and class selectors?
questions.correct: An ID selector outranks a class selector within the same cascade origin/layer
questions.wrong2: IDs and classes have identical specificity
questions.explanation: ID specificity normally outweighs class specificity within comparable cascade contexts.

questions.text: Which CSS property changes the gap between grid columns?
questions.correct: column-gap
questions.explanation: column-gap controls spacing between grid columns.

questions.text: In `box-sizing: border-box`, what does an assigned width include?
questions.correct: Content, padding and border
questions.explanation: Border-box width measures the border box; margin remains outside.

questions.text: Which CSS layout system is best suited to a two-dimensional row-and-column layout?
questions.correct: CSS Grid
questions.explanation: Grid supports explicit rows and columns.

questions.text: What determines the stacking order when positioned elements have comparable stacking contexts?
questions.correct: Stacking context rules and z-index
questions.explanation: z-index is interpreted within stacking contexts, not as one global ordering.

questions.text: What does `display: flex` establish?
questions.correct: A flex formatting context for child layout
questions.explanation: Flexbox arranges items along a main axis with cross-axis alignment.

questions.text: Why might a flex item's text overflow despite `flex-shrink: 1`?
questions.correct: Its automatic minimum size can resist shrinking
questions.wrong3: The browser ignores width rules on all text
questions.explanation: min-width: 0 can allow long content in a flex item to shrink.

questions.text: Which CSS unit is relative to the root element's font size?
questions.correct: rem
questions.explanation: rem is based on the root element's computed font size.

questions.text: What does `prefers-reduced-motion` allow?
questions.correct: Adapt animations to users requesting reduced motion
questions.wrong1: Force a higher GPU frame rate
questions.explanation: The media query responds to an accessibility motion preference.

questions.text: Which selector targets a focused input element?
questions.correct: input:focus
questions.explanation: The :focus pseudo-class matches focused controls.

questions.text: Why can `visibility: hidden` differ from `display: none`?
questions.correct: Hidden elements retain layout space; display none removes their box
questions.wrong2: Visibility hidden removes the DOM node
questions.wrong3: Display none preserves keyboard focus automatically
questions.explanation: visibility affects rendering while display none removes the box from layout.

questions.text: What does an HTML form's `method="post"` typically mean?
questions.correct: Submit form data in the request body
questions.wrong2: Send data only as URL fragments
questions.explanation: POST generally carries form data in the request body.

questions.text: Why should ARIA roles not replace correct native HTML controls unnecessarily?
questions.correct: Native elements already provide built-in semantics and keyboard behavior
questions.wrong3: Native input controls cannot be styled
questions.explanation: Use native interactive elements first; ARIA does not add missing behavior.

questions.text: Which SQL clause filters rows before grouping?
questions.correct: WHERE
questions.explanation: WHERE restricts source rows before aggregates are evaluated.

questions.text: Why can a parameterized SQL query prevent injection?
questions.correct: Parameter values are separated from SQL syntax
questions.explanation: Prepared parameters are data, not executable SQL code.

questions.text: What does an HTTP 201 status commonly indicate?
questions.correct: Resource successfully created
questions.explanation: 201 Created reports successful resource creation.

questions.text: What is the practical advantage of a database unique constraint?
questions.correct: It enforces uniqueness even under concurrent writes
questions.wrong1: It speeds every query to O(1)
questions.explanation: A database constraint preserves uniqueness across transactions.

questions.text: Which HTTP method is defined to be idempotent when implemented according to its semantics?
questions.correct: PUT
questions.explanation: Repeated PUT requests should have the same intended effect as one request.

questions.text: Why should an API validate resource ownership after authenticating a user?
questions.correct: Authentication alone does not authorize access to another user's object
questions.wrong1: All authenticated users have equal rights
questions.wrong2: Resource IDs are secret tokens by definition
questions.explanation: Object-level authorization protects user and tenant boundaries.

questions.text: What is the role of a foreign key in a relational schema?
questions.correct: Enforce references to valid parent rows
questions.explanation: Foreign keys help preserve referential integrity.

questions.text: What is optimistic concurrency control often based on?
questions.correct: Checking a version token before applying an update
questions.wrong1: Holding every row lock for an entire user session
questions.explanation: Version-based updates detect conflicts without long-lived locks.

questions.text: What is a REST resource identifier typically represented by?
questions.correct: A URI
questions.explanation: Resource URIs identify items or collections handled by an API.

questions.text: Why can retries after a timed-out POST create duplicates?
questions.correct: The server may have committed before the client saw the response
questions.wrong1: A timeout always rolls back server transactions
questions.wrong3: POST is guaranteed idempotent by default
questions.explanation: An idempotency key lets servers recognize repeated create attempts.

questions.text: What does JSON stand for?
questions.correct: JavaScript Object Notation
questions.explanation: JSON is a language-independent structured data format.

questions.text: Why can a transaction deadlock arise under concurrent updates?
questions.correct: Transactions acquire locks in conflicting orders
questions.wrong3: SQL always executes statements in parallel
questions.explanation: Lock ordering can produce cycles of waiting transactions.

questions.text: Why can returning a reference to a local automatic variable be unsafe?
questions.correct: The referenced object is destroyed when the function exits
questions.wrong3: C++ automatically extends every local lifetime
questions.explanation: An automatic local normally ceases to exist after return.

questions.text: What does `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>` provide?
questions.correct: Scope-based locking and unlocking
questions.wrong2: Automatic deadlock prevention for all lock orders
questions.explanation: The guard acquires a mutex and releases it in its destructor.

questions.text: Why does `dict.get(key, default)` differ from `dict[key]`?
questions.correct: get returns a default on a missing key instead of raising KeyError
questions.explanation: Dictionary get handles missing keys with a specified fallback.

questions.text: What does `yield from iterable` primarily provide in a generator?
questions.correct: Delegate yielded values to a sub-iterator
questions.wrong1: Convert a generator into a list immediately
questions.explanation: yield from delegates iteration to another iterator.

questions.text: What is the difference between `Array.filter` and `Array.find`?
questions.correct: filter returns all matches as an array; find returns the first match or undefined
questions.wrong2: find always mutates the original array
questions.wrong3: filter always stops after the first match
questions.explanation: filter collects matches; find searches until one match is located.

questions.text: How can `Promise.allSettled` differ from `Promise.all`?
questions.correct: It reports each outcome without rejecting solely because a member rejected
questions.explanation: allSettled waits for and reports every promise's settled status.

questions.text: Which condition makes Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm unsafe without modification?
questions.correct: Negative-weight edges
questions.wrong2: A graph with cycles of positive weight
questions.explanation: Standard Dijkstra assumes nonnegative edge weights.

questions.text: Why is a trie useful for prefix-based word search?
questions.correct: It shares common prefixes across stored strings
questions.wrong2: It stores all characters in one scalar
questions.explanation: Trie nodes represent prefixes, allowing efficient prefix traversal.

questions.text: What is the effect of `position: sticky` when its scroll threshold is reached?
questions.correct: The element behaves as sticky within its containing scroll constraints
questions.wrong1: It becomes an absolute child of the document forever
questions.wrong2: It is automatically removed from normal flow
questions.wrong3: It stops responding to all CSS
questions.explanation: Sticky positioning follows flow until an inset constraint causes it to stick.

questions.text: Why does a viewport meta tag matter for responsive mobile layouts?
questions.correct: It helps control the initial mobile layout viewport width and scale
questions.wrong3: It compiles media queries into JavaScript
questions.explanation: Mobile browsers use viewport metadata when determining layout scale.

questions.text: What does a 409 HTTP status often convey?
questions.correct: A request conflicts with current resource state
questions.wrong2: The server has no internet connection
questions.explanation: 409 Conflict indicates a state conflict that can require client resolution.

questions.text: Why can a composite index on (A, B) be less useful for filters on B alone?
questions.correct: Its leading key ordering is by A
questions.wrong1: All indexes store only one column
questions.wrong2: B is removed from the index
questions.explanation: Many B-only searches cannot efficiently use the leading key prefix.

name: Cyber Security
description: Security foundations, cryptography, web security, identity and incident response.

questions.text: What does the CIA triad stand for?
questions.correct: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
questions.explanation: The CIA triad identifies three fundamental security objectives.

questions.text: Why is the principle of least privilege important?
questions.correct: It limits accounts to permissions necessary for their tasks
questions.wrong1: It grants every user administrator rights
questions.wrong2: It removes the need for monitoring
questions.wrong3: It ensures software has no vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: Restricting rights reduces impact of compromised users and services.

questions.text: What is the difference between a threat and a vulnerability?
questions.correct: A threat can cause harm; a vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited
questions.wrong1: Both mean the same encryption method
questions.wrong3: Vulnerabilities always imply an active attack
questions.explanation: A threat source may exploit a weakness and create risk.

questions.text: What does risk assessment generally combine?
questions.correct: Likelihood and impact of an adverse event
questions.wrong3: Encryption key size and network address
questions.explanation: Risk estimates the probability and consequences of unwanted events.

questions.text: What is attack surface?
questions.correct: The exposed entry points an adversary could target
questions.wrong2: The physical size of its servers
questions.explanation: Attack surface includes reachable interfaces, services and exposed data.

questions.text: Why is defense in depth preferable to a single security control?
questions.correct: Independent layers reduce dependence on one control's success
questions.wrong2: All layers must use the same credentials
questions.explanation: Multiple controls limit the consequences of bypassing one layer.

questions.text: What is a security policy?
questions.correct: A documented set of organizational security requirements
questions.explanation: Policies communicate expected security responsibilities and controls.

questions.text: Why must vulnerability severity be evaluated in system context?
questions.correct: Exploitability, exposure and business impact vary by deployment
questions.wrong1: CVSS always predicts the exact cost of an attack
questions.wrong3: A high CVSS score means the system was compromised
questions.explanation: Severity scores inform decisions but environmental context matters.

questions.text: What is social engineering?
questions.correct: Manipulating people into unsafe actions or disclosure
questions.explanation: Social engineering exploits human trust and decision-making.

questions.text: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.correct: Authentication confirms identity; authorization determines permitted actions
questions.explanation: Identity verification precedes decisions about access rights.

questions.text: What is a zero-trust security principle?
questions.correct: Verify access continuously rather than assume network location is trusted
questions.wrong1: Trust every internal device by default
questions.wrong3: Treat VPN access as unrestricted authorization
questions.explanation: Zero trust emphasizes explicit verification and least-privilege access.

questions.text: Why should security logging avoid collecting raw passwords or private keys?
questions.correct: Secrets in logs increase exposure and breach impact
questions.wrong2: Logs are always invisible to administrators
questions.wrong3: Password values have no sensitive meaning
questions.explanation: Logs should provide audit evidence without unnecessarily storing secrets.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a security baseline?
questions.correct: Establish a minimum approved configuration
questions.explanation: Baselines define expected security settings for consistent hardening.

questions.text: Why is separating production and development credentials useful?
questions.correct: It limits compromise scope and accidental access
questions.wrong1: It ensures code has no defects
questions.explanation: Environment separation prevents development secrets from granting production access.

questions.text: What does a vulnerability scanner primarily do?
questions.correct: Identify potential weaknesses requiring validation
questions.explanation: Automated scans find indicators and need contextual verification.

questions.text: What is the difference between a security event and a confirmed incident?
questions.correct: An event is an observation; an incident requires evidence of relevant security impact or violation
questions.wrong2: An incident is always a false alarm
questions.wrong3: Events cannot be collected by monitoring systems
questions.explanation: Alert triage distinguishes signals from substantiated security incidents.

questions.text: What does data minimization mean?
questions.correct: Collect and retain only necessary personal data
questions.explanation: Data minimization reduces the volume of personal information processed.

questions.text: Why should threat modeling occur before a system is deployed?
questions.correct: Design flaws can be addressed before they become costly to change
questions.wrong1: It eliminates every software defect automatically
questions.wrong2: Only post-deployment logs identify trust boundaries
questions.wrong3: Threat modeling is needed only for hardware
questions.explanation: Threat modeling identifies assets, adversaries and trust boundaries during design.

questions.text: What is the role of an asset inventory in cybersecurity?
questions.correct: Track systems and software that require protection
questions.wrong2: Assign random IP addresses to every laptop
questions.explanation: Defenders must know what systems and components they operate.

questions.text: What does a compensating control provide?
questions.correct: An alternative risk-reduction measure when the preferred control cannot be implemented
questions.wrong1: An exemption from all security requirements
questions.wrong2: A guarantee of zero residual risk
questions.wrong3: An additional unencrypted copy of secrets
questions.explanation: Compensating controls help achieve security objectives via alternative mechanisms.

questions.text: Which property does hashing primarily provide for checking data integrity?
questions.correct: A compact digest that changes when input changes
questions.wrong1: Reversible encryption using a shared secret
questions.explanation: Cryptographic hashes support integrity checks but do not inherently authenticate the sender.

questions.text: Why should user passwords be hashed with an adaptive password-hashing algorithm?
questions.correct: It makes large-scale guessing more expensive
questions.wrong2: It removes the need for unique salts
questions.wrong3: It makes passwords immune to phishing
questions.explanation: Argon2, scrypt or bcrypt slow down offline guessing compared with fast hashes.

questions.text: What is a salt in password hashing?
questions.correct: A unique nonsecret value mixed into each password hash
questions.explanation: A salt reduces the effectiveness of precomputed rainbow tables and separates equal passwords.

questions.text: What is the consequence of nonce reuse with AES-GCM under the same key?
questions.correct: Confidentiality and integrity can be seriously compromised
questions.explanation: GCM requires unique nonces for a given encryption key.

questions.text: Which cryptographic technique uses the same shared secret for encryption and decryption?
questions.correct: Symmetric encryption
questions.explanation: Symmetric algorithms encrypt and decrypt with a shared secret key.

questions.text: Why do digital signatures differ from message authentication codes?
questions.correct: Signatures allow verification with a public key rather than a shared secret
questions.wrong3: MACs can be verified anonymously by everyone
questions.explanation: Digital signatures provide public-key verifiability; MACs use shared-key authentication.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a certificate authority in TLS?
questions.correct: Bind public keys to identities through signed certificates
questions.explanation: Trusted CAs sign certificates that help authenticate endpoints.

questions.text: What does forward secrecy protect against?
questions.correct: Past session confidentiality if long-term keys are compromised later
questions.explanation: Ephemeral key exchange can prevent later key compromise from decrypting earlier sessions.

questions.text: What is an HMAC?
questions.correct: A keyed message authentication code constructed from a hash
questions.explanation: HMAC authenticates data using a shared secret and hash function.

questions.text: Why is authenticated encryption preferable to encryption without integrity protection?
questions.correct: It can detect unauthorized ciphertext modification
questions.wrong3: It removes the need for secure key storage
questions.explanation: AEAD combines confidentiality with integrity and authenticity checks.

questions.text: What does a cryptographic digital signature primarily verify?
questions.correct: Message integrity and possession of the corresponding signing key
questions.wrong1: The truthfulness of the signed statement
questions.wrong3: The physical location of the signer
questions.explanation: Signature verification authenticates key-based origin and detects modification.

questions.text: Why should encryption keys be rotated after suspected compromise?
questions.correct: Further use of the compromised key can expose new data
questions.wrong1: Rotation guarantees previously stolen data is recovered
questions.explanation: Replacing compromised keys limits subsequent exposure but does not undo historical leaks.

questions.text: Which operation is generally infeasible for a secure one-way hash?
questions.correct: Reconstructing arbitrary original inputs from the digest
questions.wrong1: Computing a digest from a message
questions.wrong3: Storing a digest in a database
questions.explanation: Preimage resistance makes reversing the hash computationally difficult.

questions.text: What does collision resistance mean for a cryptographic hash?
questions.correct: It is hard to find any two distinct inputs with the same digest
questions.wrong1: No two inputs can ever share a digest mathematically
questions.wrong2: The hash can always be decrypted
questions.wrong3: Every input has a unique secret key
questions.explanation: Finite digests can collide; resistance means finding collisions is impractical.

questions.text: What does encryption at rest protect primarily?
questions.correct: Stored data against unauthorized reading when storage is exposed
questions.explanation: At-rest encryption protects storage media and backups subject to key handling.

questions.text: Why is hard-coding encryption keys into a public repository unsafe?
questions.correct: Anyone with repository access can obtain the keys
questions.wrong2: Keys become cryptographically stronger when visible
questions.wrong3: Source code cannot contain string constants
questions.explanation: Secrets should be stored in dedicated secret-management systems.

questions.text: Which algorithm is asymmetric?
questions.correct: RSA
questions.explanation: RSA uses public/private key operations.

questions.text: What does key derivation from a password typically require?
questions.correct: A salt and a deliberately costly derivation process
questions.wrong1: An ordinary fast MD5 call only
questions.wrong2: Storing the original plaintext password next to the key
questions.wrong3: A fixed publicly known output key for all users
questions.explanation: Strong password-based derivation slows attackers and derives consistent key material.

questions.text: What is a certificate revocation mechanism intended to indicate?
questions.correct: A certificate should no longer be trusted before expiry
questions.wrong2: A symmetric key is too short to use
questions.wrong3: A user forgot the system password
questions.explanation: Revocation mechanisms communicate certificate invalidation.

questions.text: What does a cryptographic key-management lifecycle include?
questions.correct: Generation, storage, rotation, revocation and destruction
questions.wrong1: Only choosing a sufficiently long filename
questions.explanation: Secure keys require protection from creation through retirement.

questions.text: What is SQL injection?
questions.correct: Untrusted input alters the structure of a database query
questions.wrong3: Splitting a SQL table by date
questions.explanation: SQL injection occurs when data is interpreted as query syntax.

questions.text: Which defense most directly prevents SQL injection in ordinary application queries?
questions.correct: Parameterized statements with strict value binding
questions.wrong3: Putting SQL behind a reverse proxy
questions.explanation: Prepared queries keep user values separate from SQL instructions.

questions.text: What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
questions.correct: Untrusted data executes as script in a user's browser
questions.wrong1: A password is sent using a TLS connection
questions.wrong2: A server uses a CSS stylesheet
questions.wrong3: An image is cached by a CDN
questions.explanation: XSS arises when attacker-controlled content reaches unsafe browser execution contexts.

questions.text: Why is HTML output encoding context-dependent?
questions.correct: HTML text, attributes, URLs and JavaScript contexts require different rules
questions.wrong1: One generic escape function handles every context perfectly
questions.explanation: Safe output encoding matches the syntax of the insertion context.

questions.text: What does CSRF exploit?
questions.correct: A victim's browser sends an unintended authenticated request
questions.wrong1: The server's RAM has too little space
questions.explanation: CSRF abuses automatic browser credentials on cross-site requests.

questions.text: How do anti-CSRF tokens help?
questions.correct: They bind state-changing requests to an authorized session or form
questions.wrong2: They automatically authorize every user role
questions.wrong3: They encrypt request payloads end to end
questions.explanation: Servers verify tokens not reasonably available to unauthorized cross-site requesters.

questions.text: What is broken object-level authorization?
questions.correct: A user accesses another user's object due to missing access checks
questions.explanation: BOLA occurs when resource ownership or permissions are not enforced.

questions.text: Why is merely hiding an admin button not an authorization control?
questions.correct: Users can call the backend route directly
questions.wrong1: Hidden HTML elements are cryptographically protected
questions.wrong3: Only JavaScript can send HTTP requests
questions.explanation: Server endpoints must independently enforce roles and ownership.

questions.text: What is a Content Security Policy mainly used for?
questions.correct: Restrict which resources and scripts a browser may execute or load
questions.explanation: CSP limits some injection impacts by defining approved content sources.

questions.text: Why is the HttpOnly cookie attribute helpful?
questions.correct: It blocks direct cookie access by page JavaScript
questions.wrong2: It requires the browser to use HTTPS automatically
questions.wrong3: It sets the user's password strength
questions.explanation: HttpOnly reduces JavaScript-based session cookie theft but not all session misuse.

questions.text: What does the Secure attribute on a cookie require in supporting browsers?
questions.correct: The cookie is sent only over HTTPS
questions.wrong2: The cookie is encrypted in the database
questions.wrong3: The cookie is always inaccessible to scripts
questions.explanation: Secure restricts cookie transmission to secure channels.

questions.text: What risk does unrestricted file upload introduce?
questions.correct: Malicious files or resource exhaustion can reach the server
questions.wrong1: Every uploaded file is harmless if renamed
questions.wrong3: File extension checks guarantee full validation
questions.explanation: Uploads require size, signature, content, storage and access controls.

questions.text: What is rate limiting intended to restrict?
questions.correct: How frequently a client may invoke an endpoint
questions.wrong1: Which CPU instruction set is installed
questions.wrong2: The number of HTML elements on a page
questions.explanation: Rate limits reduce abuse and resource exhaustion.

questions.text: Why is accepting only the browser-provided `isAdmin=true` field insecure?
questions.correct: The client can forge its own claimed privileges
questions.explanation: Authorization decisions must rely on server-trusted identity and policy.

questions.text: What is SSRF?
questions.correct: A server is induced to make unintended requests to targets
questions.wrong1: A browser is forced into fullscreen
