questions.wrong2: A user reuses an old password
questions.wrong3: A TLS key is rotated too early
questions.explanation: Server-side request forgery abuses outbound requests made by backend services.

questions.text: Why should server-side URL fetchers restrict destinations?
questions.correct: They might otherwise access internal metadata or privileged services
questions.wrong1: All public URLs are inherently malicious
questions.explanation: Destination controls reduce SSRF exposure to sensitive internal targets.

questions.text: What is session fixation?
questions.correct: An attacker tries to make a victim use a session identifier the attacker knows
questions.wrong1: The server rotates every session ID on login
questions.wrong2: A browser refuses to save cookies
questions.wrong3: A user's password is changed automatically
questions.explanation: Fixation exploits failure to refresh identifiers when authentication context changes.

questions.text: Why should sessions be regenerated after login?
questions.correct: It prevents a pre-login identifier from being retained as an authenticated session
questions.wrong3: It guarantees no user can be impersonated
questions.explanation: Renewing identifiers mitigates session fixation.

questions.text: What does a 403 Forbidden response normally indicate?
questions.correct: The request is understood but access is denied
questions.wrong3: The user must change the DNS resolver
questions.explanation: 403 signifies insufficient access to the requested resource.

questions.text: What does a security-relevant audit trail need for trustworthy review?
questions.correct: Consistent timestamps, event IDs and controlled write access
questions.wrong3: The ability for all users to delete entries
questions.explanation: Tamper-resistant event context supports incident investigation.

questions.text: What is multi-factor authentication?
questions.correct: Using two or more distinct authentication factor categories
questions.explanation: MFA combines categories such as knowledge, possession and inherence.

questions.text: Why do two passwords not qualify as two distinct authentication factors?
questions.correct: Both are knowledge factors
questions.wrong2: One password automatically counts as possession
questions.wrong3: MFA requires every factor to be public
questions.explanation: Factor diversity reduces dependence on one type of secret.

questions.text: What does RBAC use to control permissions?
questions.correct: Assigned roles
questions.explanation: Role-based access control maps permissions to roles assigned to subjects.

questions.text: What is attribute-based access control (ABAC)?
questions.correct: Permissions evaluated from user, resource, action and environment attributes
questions.wrong1: Authorization solely from a single username
questions.explanation: ABAC policies use contextual attributes to decide access.

questions.text: What is phishing?
questions.correct: Deceptive communication used to steal information or induce unsafe actions
questions.explanation: Phishing impersonates trusted parties to manipulate recipients.

questions.text: Why are passkeys generally more phishing resistant than reusable passwords?
questions.correct: They use origin-bound public-key authentication
questions.wrong1: They send the private key to every site
questions.wrong2: They work only with a memorized secret
questions.explanation: WebAuthn credentials bind authenticator responses to the relying party origin.

questions.text: What does a password manager primarily help with?
questions.correct: Generating and storing unique strong passwords
questions.explanation: Managers support strong unique passwords and reduce reuse.

questions.text: Why should account recovery receive security controls comparable to login?
questions.correct: Attackers may bypass strong login by abusing weaker recovery paths
questions.wrong2: All recovery messages are encrypted automatically
questions.wrong3: Recovery is available only to administrators
questions.explanation: Recovery paths can become an alternative route to account takeover.

questions.text: What is the principle of separation of duties?
questions.correct: Split sensitive responsibilities across roles or individuals
questions.wrong1: Give one person every administrative power
questions.explanation: Separating duties reduces fraud and accidental misuse.

questions.text: Why should API tokens have narrowly scoped permissions?
questions.correct: A leaked token then grants fewer capabilities
questions.explanation: Fine-grained scopes reduce the damage of credential exposure.

questions.text: What is credential stuffing?
questions.correct: Trying known leaked username/password combinations on other services
questions.wrong1: Generating unique credentials in a manager
questions.explanation: Credential stuffing exploits password reuse across sites.

questions.text: Why can login throttling be necessary even with strong password hashing?
questions.correct: Online attempts still need protection from automation
questions.wrong3: Passwords cannot be guessed through HTTP
questions.explanation: Rate limits mitigate repeated online credential attacks.

questions.text: What does a hardware security key often provide?
questions.correct: A possession-based authentication factor
questions.explanation: Hardware authenticators protect private credentials and confirm possession.

questions.text: Why must an access token's signature and claims both be validated?
questions.correct: A valid signature alone does not guarantee correct issuer, audience or expiry
questions.wrong1: Signatures are only for file compression
questions.wrong3: Token expiry is enforced by DNS
questions.explanation: Secure validation checks cryptographic authenticity and application constraints.

questions.text: What is an authorization bypass?
questions.correct: Accessing a protected action without satisfying its permission checks
questions.explanation: Authorization bypasses exploit missing or flawed access enforcement.

questions.text: Why do JWTs not automatically provide confidentiality?
questions.correct: Their payloads are commonly just encoded and signed, not encrypted
questions.wrong1: All JWTs require a shared AES key
questions.explanation: A signed JWT is usually readable unless separately encrypted.

questions.text: What is the purpose of reauthentication before a sensitive account change?
questions.correct: Confirm the user's continued control of their session
questions.explanation: Step-up authentication reduces risk from unattended or compromised sessions.

questions.text: Why should privileged operations require server-side permission rechecks?
questions.correct: Roles and permissions may change after the session was established
questions.wrong1: All roles are permanently fixed at registration
questions.explanation: Server checks prevent stale or forged client state from granting power.

questions.text: What does an identity provider (IdP) usually handle?
questions.correct: Authentication and identity assertions
questions.explanation: An IdP authenticates users and issues claims or tokens to relying services.

questions.text: Why is a short-lived access token safer than an indefinite token?
questions.correct: Compromise can grant access for a shorter interval
questions.wrong2: Short tokens remove the need for TLS
questions.explanation: Limited lifetimes restrict the period a stolen token remains useful.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of security patch management?
questions.correct: Reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: Updates remediate disclosed or discovered security flaws.

questions.text: Why should software patches be tested before broad rollout?
questions.correct: Compatibility failures can cause service outages
questions.explanation: Staged rollout reduces operational risk while maintaining urgency.

questions.text: What is an indicator of compromise (IOC)?
questions.correct: An observable artifact that may indicate malicious activity
questions.explanation: IOCs include suspicious hashes, domains, processes or activity patterns.

questions.text: Why does an IOC alone not prove a security breach?
questions.correct: Indicators can be ambiguous or produce false positives
questions.wrong1: All IOCs are issued by attackers
questions.wrong2: IOCs are always private encryption keys
questions.wrong3: Network logs contain no contextual information
questions.explanation: Incident confirmation requires contextual evidence beyond one indicator.

questions.text: What is an incident-response playbook?
questions.correct: A documented sequence of actions for a scenario
questions.explanation: Playbooks guide consistent handling of known incident types.

questions.text: Why is evidence chain of custody important?
questions.correct: It documents collection, handling and integrity of evidence
questions.wrong2: It provides network encryption for free
questions.explanation: Traceable custody supports reliable incident review.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a SIEM platform?
questions.correct: Aggregate and correlate security logs and events
questions.wrong1: Compile every application on the network
questions.explanation: SIEM platforms centralize telemetry for monitoring and investigation.

questions.text: What is the distinction between RTO and RPO?
questions.correct: RTO is target recovery time; RPO is acceptable data-loss window
questions.explanation: Recovery time and recovery point objectives describe different continuity requirements.

questions.text: What does an offline backup help protect against?
questions.correct: Ransomware encrypting reachable backup copies
questions.explanation: Disconnected backups may remain safe when online systems are compromised.

questions.text: Why are regular restore tests necessary even when backups report success?
questions.correct: Backup completion does not prove data can be restored correctly
questions.wrong1: Testing removes the need for encryption
questions.wrong2: Backups can only fail in the cloud
questions.explanation: Restore exercises validate usable recovery paths.

questions.text: What is endpoint detection and response (EDR)?
questions.correct: Monitoring and investigating endpoint activity
questions.explanation: EDR tools collect endpoint telemetry and support response actions.

questions.text: Why should malware containment precede some remediation tasks?
questions.correct: Active threats may spread while systems remain connected
questions.explanation: Isolation can limit attacker movement and additional compromise.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a firewall deny-by-default approach?
questions.correct: Allow only explicitly authorized network flows
questions.wrong1: Permit every service unless blocked later
questions.explanation: A restrictive default reduces unintended exposure.

questions.text: Why do organizations separate detection latency from response latency?
questions.correct: Finding an incident and taking action are different time intervals
questions.explanation: Measuring both reveals distinct operational delays.

questions.text: What does a false positive security alert mean?
questions.correct: A benign condition was incorrectly flagged as malicious
questions.explanation: False positives impose investigation cost without actual malicious activity.

questions.text: What risk can excessive alert volume create?
questions.correct: Alert fatigue causes genuine incidents to be overlooked
questions.wrong2: No event can be logged after 100 alerts
questions.explanation: Prioritization and deduplication help analysts attend to actionable signals.

questions.text: What is an incident severity classification used for?
questions.correct: Prioritize response based on impact and urgency
questions.explanation: Severity levels guide escalation and resource allocation.

questions.text: Why should production monitoring include both health and security metrics?
questions.correct: A component outage can look like absence of attacks without actual visibility
questions.wrong1: Security logs always reveal CPU deadlocks
questions.wrong3: Monitoring is reliable whenever HTTP returns 200
questions.explanation: Operational telemetry helps distinguish quiet systems from failed detectors.

questions.text: What is secure configuration management intended to prevent?
questions.correct: Drift from approved baseline settings
questions.explanation: Configuration controls help detect and correct unintended changes.

questions.text: Why does immutable audit storage help post-incident analysis?
questions.correct: It makes undetected alteration of recorded events harder
questions.wrong2: It can never run out of space
questions.wrong3: It removes the need for access control
questions.explanation: Tamper-resistant logging preserves trustworthy historical evidence.

questions.text: How does privacy by design differ from adding privacy controls after deployment?
questions.correct: It integrates data protection into architecture from the start
questions.wrong1: It prohibits all processing of personal information
questions.wrong2: It requires collecting every possible data field
questions.wrong3: It is limited to screen layout
questions.explanation: Early privacy design influences data flows, access and retention decisions.

questions.text: Why should a security design identify trust boundaries?
questions.correct: Data crossing boundaries may need additional validation and authorization
questions.wrong1: All traffic inside one network is safe
questions.wrong2: Boundaries only matter for paper documents
questions.wrong3: Trust boundaries eliminate the need for logging
questions.explanation: Trust changes at boundaries such as browser-to-server and service-to-database.

questions.text: What is the shared responsibility principle in cloud security?
questions.correct: Provider and customer control different layers of the environment
questions.wrong1: The cloud provider secures every application account automatically
questions.wrong2: Customers must manage the provider's physical datacenters
questions.wrong3: Responsibility always belongs to a single team
questions.explanation: Customer duties commonly include identities, configuration and workloads.

questions.text: Why is a risk register useful beyond a single audit?
questions.correct: It tracks owners, mitigation decisions and residual risk over time
questions.wrong1: It guarantees no incidents will happen
questions.wrong2: It serves as an encryption key vault
questions.explanation: Continuous tracking makes outstanding risks visible and accountable.

questions.text: Why should comparisons of cryptographic authentication tags use constant-time techniques?
questions.correct: Variable comparison timing may leak secret-dependent information
questions.wrong1: Constant time always makes code run faster
questions.wrong2: It removes the need for a secret key
questions.explanation: Timing-safe comparisons reduce information leakage through early exits.

questions.text: What property does a secure random number generator need for key generation?
questions.correct: Unpredictable outputs with sufficient entropy
questions.wrong1: The same sequence at every process start
questions.explanation: Predictable random numbers can expose generated secrets.

questions.text: Why is ECB mode generally unsuitable for encrypting structured images?
questions.correct: Equal plaintext blocks can produce equal ciphertext patterns
questions.wrong2: ECB always loses half the data
questions.explanation: ECB reveals repeated-block patterns and lacks authenticated protection.

questions.text: Why should a password reset token have a short expiry and single-use semantics?
questions.correct: A stolen or replayed token then has limited usefulness
questions.wrong3: Tokens cannot be intercepted under TLS
questions.explanation: Expiry and one-time consumption limit account takeover opportunities.

questions.text: Why is a CSRF token inadequate as the only defense against XSS?
questions.correct: An injected same-origin script may access or use token-bearing requests
questions.wrong1: CSRF tokens are designed to encrypt JavaScript
questions.explanation: CSRF and XSS target different threats and need separate controls.

questions.text: What does secure file-upload storage outside the web root achieve?
questions.correct: Uploaded files cannot be directly requested as public static assets
questions.explanation: Protected storage requires controlled download endpoints and permission checks.

questions.text: Why must servers reject unexpected HTTP methods on sensitive routes?
questions.correct: Alternate methods may bypass assumptions in routing and authorization
questions.wrong2: GET is always encrypted while POST is not
questions.explanation: Explicit allowed-method validation reduces unintended operations.

questions.text: Why should API error responses avoid exposing SQL stack traces?
questions.correct: Implementation details can help attackers while leaking internal data
questions.wrong2: Traces are always encrypted by the browser
questions.wrong3: Errors must contain raw credentials for troubleshooting
questions.explanation: Server logs can retain details while clients receive sanitized errors.

questions.text: Why should authorization decisions be made per exam and per student rather than only per teacher role?
questions.correct: Teacher role alone does not establish access to every candidate's private records
questions.wrong1: All teachers own all exams by design
questions.wrong2: A question ID is a secure access token
questions.explanation: Object-level permissions enforce exam ownership and explicit invigilation rights.

questions.text: Why is session revocation important after a password reset?
questions.correct: Existing stolen sessions may otherwise remain usable
questions.wrong2: It rotates all TLS certificates automatically
questions.wrong3: It changes every database primary key
questions.explanation: Revoking sessions can cut off access from previously compromised credentials.

questions.text: What is the advantage of just-in-time privileged access?
questions.correct: Elevated rights exist only for a limited approved period
questions.explanation: Temporary elevation shrinks the window of excessive privilege.

questions.text: Why are biometric matching scores not the same as definitive personal identity proof?
questions.correct: Models have error rates and depend on image quality and presentation attacks
questions.wrong1: Every biometric score is legally conclusive
questions.wrong3: Scores can be interpreted without thresholds
questions.explanation: Identity decisions require validated thresholds and suitable challenge/evidence policies.

questions.text: How can an attacker benefit when monitoring stops but the dashboard shows green?
questions.correct: Loss of visibility is incorrectly presented as normal activity
questions.wrong1: Monitoring failures prove no attack occurred
questions.explanation: Healthy, uncertain and disconnected states should be distinguished.

questions.text: Why should incident evidence have a stable event ID?
questions.correct: It reliably links timestamps, alerts and media across services
questions.wrong2: It replaces permissions on the media
questions.wrong3: It allows duplicate alerts to be counted as new incidents
questions.explanation: Stable identifiers support correlation and idempotent upload handling.

questions.text: What is an evidence retention policy intended to specify?
questions.correct: How long records are kept, protected and eventually disposed of
questions.wrong1: The number of screens a user may connect
questions.wrong2: Only the size of database indexes
questions.wrong3: How often to change the CSS theme
questions.explanation: Defined retention limits excess sensitive data while meeting legitimate obligations.

questions.text: Why do independent health checks matter in a multi-service AI monitoring system?
questions.correct: One worker failure should not silently hide other services' status
questions.wrong1: All services can share one success flag safely
questions.wrong2: Every backend must block on slow video uploads
questions.wrong3: A single HTTP 200 proves all models performed inference
questions.explanation: Per-service health and latency make degraded components visible.

name: AI, ML, Deep Learning & Data Science
description: Artificial intelligence, ML, deep learning, statistics, evaluation and MLOps.

questions.text: What distinguishes supervised learning from unsupervised learning?
questions.correct: Supervised training uses labeled target outcomes
questions.wrong3: Unsupervised learning can only use images
questions.explanation: Supervised models learn mappings from examples with targets.

questions.text: What is the main conceptual difference between narrow AI and artificial general intelligence?
questions.correct: Narrow AI specializes in tasks; AGI would generalize broadly across domains
questions.wrong2: AGI is a standard installed Python package
questions.wrong3: Narrow AI never learns from data
questions.explanation: AGI refers to broad general-purpose intelligence, not a current guaranteed capability.

questions.text: Which algorithm is an example of a graph search strategy?
questions.correct: A* search
questions.explanation: A* searches graph paths using costs and a heuristic.

questions.text: When is an A* search heuristic admissible?
questions.correct: It never overestimates the true remaining optimal cost
questions.wrong1: It always equals the final path cost
questions.wrong2: It always overestimates to speed search
questions.wrong3: It has to be constant for every node
questions.explanation: Admissible heuristics are lower bounds on remaining path cost.

questions.text: What is an expert system's knowledge base used for?
questions.correct: Represent domain facts or rules
questions.explanation: Expert systems apply inference rules to encoded knowledge.

questions.text: What is a major limitation of purely rule-based AI in open-ended environments?
questions.correct: Maintaining comprehensive rules for novel cases is difficult
questions.wrong1: Rules cannot be executed on computers
questions.wrong3: Rules automatically learn all new concepts
questions.explanation: Rules do not necessarily adapt beyond what was encoded.

questions.text: What does an intelligent agent generally do?
questions.correct: Perceive an environment and take actions toward objectives
questions.wrong2: Always need a human to press every action
questions.explanation: Agents select actions from observations and goals.

questions.text: Why can a reward-maximizing agent exhibit unintended behavior?
questions.correct: An imperfect reward specification can incentivize undesirable shortcuts
questions.explanation: Reward design may differ from the real goal and needs safeguards.

questions.text: What is a search tree's branching factor?
questions.correct: Number of successor choices per state
questions.explanation: Branching factor describes how many alternatives each search node generates.

questions.text: Why is an approximate heuristic useful in combinatorial search?
questions.correct: It guides exploration when exhaustive search is expensive
questions.wrong1: It guarantees the optimal answer for every algorithm
questions.wrong2: It removes all graph cycles automatically
questions.explanation: Heuristics prioritize promising states to reduce explored possibilities.

questions.text: What is an ontology in knowledge representation?
questions.correct: A structured description of concepts and relationships
questions.explanation: Ontologies encode entities, properties and relations for reasoning.

questions.text: What is the open-world assumption in knowledge representation?
questions.correct: Missing information is not necessarily false
questions.wrong1: Anything not stored is always false
questions.explanation: Open-world systems distinguish unknown facts from explicit falsehoods.

questions.text: What does NLP stand for?
questions.correct: Natural Language Processing
questions.explanation: NLP studies computational processing of human language.

questions.text: Why do LLMs sometimes hallucinate?
questions.correct: They can generate plausible text not grounded in verified facts
questions.wrong1: Every response is retrieved from a trusted database
questions.wrong3: Large models only output exact training sentences
questions.explanation: Language modeling objectives do not guarantee factual grounding.

questions.text: What is a token in modern language modeling?
questions.correct: A unit of text processed by a tokenizer
questions.explanation: Tokenizers split text into subword, word or symbol units.

questions.text: What does temperature generally affect in token sampling?
questions.correct: The randomness of the next-token distribution
questions.explanation: Temperature rescales logits before sampling, changing diversity.

questions.text: Which technique augments an LLM response with retrieved documents?
questions.correct: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant external context before or during generation.

questions.text: Why are retrieved passages not necessarily trustworthy instructions for an AI assistant?
questions.correct: They may contain untrusted prompt injection content
questions.wrong1: Any retrieved text overrides developer rules
questions.wrong2: All retrieval sources are verified by TLS
questions.wrong3: Document text is always safe to execute
questions.explanation: Retrieval content should be treated as evidence, not as authoritative system instructions.

questions.text: What is a vector embedding used for in AI?
questions.correct: Represent objects as numerical features for comparison or prediction
questions.wrong2: Convert every image to a filename
questions.explanation: Embeddings place items in a vector space where geometric structure may carry meaning.

questions.text: Why can cosine similarity be useful for embeddings?
questions.correct: It compares vector direction independently of magnitude
questions.wrong3: It always produces the exact training label
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity uses the angle between vectors to measure directional alignment.

questions.text: What is the primary objective of linear regression?
questions.correct: Predict a continuous numeric target
questions.explanation: Linear regression models a numeric response using features.

questions.text: Why does regularization help prevent overfitting?
questions.correct: It penalizes overly complex model parameters
questions.explanation: Regularization discourages overly flexible solutions.

questions.text: Which task is commonly solved by logistic regression?
questions.correct: Binary classification
questions.explanation: Logistic regression models class probability using a logistic link.

questions.text: What does L1 regularization often encourage?
questions.correct: Sparse parameter values with some coefficients zero
questions.explanation: The absolute-value penalty can drive coefficients exactly to zero.

questions.text: What does overfitting mean?
questions.correct: A model learns training-specific patterns that generalize poorly
questions.wrong1: A model has too few parameters to learn anything
questions.explanation: Overfit models perform much better on training data than unseen examples.

questions.text: How can data leakage inflate validation accuracy?
questions.correct: Information unavailable at prediction time reaches model training or features
questions.wrong1: Data leakage lowers training sample count
questions.wrong2: It is the same as missing-value imputation only
questions.wrong3: Validation labels are always public at deployment
questions.explanation: Leakage makes evaluation unrealistically optimistic.

questions.text: Which tree ensemble trains trees sequentially to correct prior errors?
questions.correct: Gradient boosting
questions.explanation: Boosting adds models that focus on reducing the ensemble's residual errors.

questions.text: Why does random forest commonly reduce variance relative to one deep tree?
questions.correct: It averages many decorrelated tree predictions
questions.wrong1: All trees are forced to be identical
questions.wrong3: It always has lower bias on every dataset
questions.explanation: Bagging and randomized feature choices reduce correlation among high-variance trees.

questions.text: What does the k in k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) represent?
questions.correct: Number of neighbors consulted for prediction
questions.explanation: k-NN uses the nearest k training examples to infer a prediction.

questions.text: Why does distance-based classification often require feature scaling?
questions.correct: Features on larger numeric scales can dominate distance
questions.wrong1: Scaling adds more labeled training cases
questions.wrong2: It changes categorical labels to text
questions.explanation: Standardization or normalization makes distances more comparable.

questions.text: What type of decision boundary does a linear SVM learn in original feature space?
questions.correct: A hyperplane
questions.explanation: Linear support vector machines separate classes with a margin-maximizing hyperplane.

questions.text: What does the kernel trick enable in an SVM?
questions.correct: Implicit nonlinear feature-space similarity without explicitly constructing all coordinates
questions.explanation: Kernel functions express inner products in transformed feature spaces.

questions.text: What is a hyperparameter?
questions.correct: A setting chosen outside parameter fitting such as learning rate
questions.wrong1: An optimally learned weight by gradient descent
questions.explanation: Hyperparameters control model design and optimization.

questions.text: Why should hyperparameters be selected using validation rather than final test data?
questions.correct: Using test labels during tuning contaminates unbiased evaluation
questions.wrong1: Test data always contain more samples
questions.wrong2: Hyperparameters can only use integer values
questions.wrong3: Validation is never related to training
questions.explanation: A held-out test set should assess the final selected model.

questions.text: What is cross-validation used for?
questions.correct: Estimate performance across multiple train/validation splits
questions.explanation: Cross-validation evaluates how performance varies across resampled splits.

questions.text: Why may ordinary random cross-validation be inappropriate for time series?
questions.correct: It can train on future observations relative to the validation period
questions.explanation: Chronological splits preserve causal prediction order.

questions.text: What does class imbalance mean?
questions.correct: Some classes appear much less frequently than others
questions.wrong3: The dataset has no training split
questions.explanation: Imbalanced datasets have unequal target class frequencies.

questions.text: Why can accuracy be misleading for rare fraud detection?
questions.correct: Predicting the majority class can yield high accuracy while missing fraud
questions.wrong1: Accuracy always accounts equally for precision and recall
questions.explanation: Class imbalance requires metrics that expose missed positives.

questions.text: What does early stopping do?
questions.correct: Stop training when monitored validation improvement stalls
questions.explanation: Stopping based on validation performance can reduce overfitting.

questions.text: What is calibration in probabilistic classification?
questions.correct: Predicted probabilities agree with observed event frequencies
questions.wrong2: Model weights all have equal magnitude
questions.wrong3: Training is always performed at room temperature
questions.explanation: A calibrated 0.7 probability should correspond to roughly 70% positive frequency over comparable cases.

questions.text: Which algorithm groups observations into k clusters around centroids?
questions.correct: K-means
questions.explanation: K-means alternates centroid assignment and centroid update.

questions.text: Why can K-means be sensitive to outliers?
questions.correct: Squared distance gives far-away points large influence
questions.wrong3: Every cluster has exactly the same size
questions.explanation: Outliers can pull cluster centroids away from dense regions.

questions.text: What does PCA primarily seek?
questions.correct: Orthogonal directions of maximum variance
questions.explanation: Principal component analysis identifies high-variance linear axes.

questions.text: Why must PCA generally be fit only on training data?
questions.correct: Fitting it on validation/test samples leaks information about their distribution
questions.explanation: Unsupervised preprocessing can still leak evaluation data when fit globally.

questions.text: Which clustering approach can mark some points as noise?
questions.correct: DBSCAN
questions.explanation: Density-based clustering can leave isolated points unlabeled.

questions.text: How does DBSCAN differ from K-means?
questions.correct: It finds density-connected regions without specifying k in advance
questions.wrong2: It always creates convex spherical clusters
questions.explanation: DBSCAN uses density and neighborhood radius to discover clusters and noise.

questions.text: What does the silhouette score assess?
questions.correct: Within-cluster cohesion versus separation from other clusters
questions.wrong1: Accuracy against ground-truth class labels only
questions.explanation: Silhouette compares how close a point is to its cluster and the nearest alternative cluster.

questions.text: Why can high-dimensional nearest-neighbor distances become less discriminative?
questions.correct: Distances may concentrate as dimensions increase
questions.wrong1: Euclidean distance is undefined beyond three dimensions
questions.wrong3: All high-dimensional data are linearly separable
questions.explanation: The curse of dimensionality can weaken distance-based methods.

questions.text: What is reinforcement learning centered on?
questions.correct: An agent learning actions from rewards and transitions
questions.wrong1: Learning from only labeled static images
questions.explanation: RL optimizes a policy through interactions and reward feedback.

questions.text: What is the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in RL?
questions.correct: Trying uncertain actions versus choosing known high-reward actions
questions.explanation: Agents must gather information while maximizing reward.

questions.text: What is a policy in reinforcement learning?
questions.correct: A mapping from observations/states to action choices
questions.wrong1: A collection of server firewall rules only
questions.explanation: A policy specifies how an agent selects actions.

questions.text: What does the discount factor gamma affect?
questions.correct: How much future rewards contribute to expected return
questions.wrong1: How labels are encoded in one-hot vectors
questions.explanation: A lower gamma discounts delayed rewards more strongly.

questions.text: What does Q-learning estimate?
questions.correct: Expected discounted return for a state-action choice
questions.wrong2: The mean of each feature column
questions.explanation: Q-values estimate long-term reward from taking actions.

questions.text: Why is off-policy learning distinct from on-policy learning?
questions.correct: It can learn about a target policy using data from a different behavior policy
questions.wrong1: It cannot learn from old experiences
questions.explanation: Off-policy methods can train from behavior that differs from the policy being improved.

questions.text: What is a reward signal?
questions.correct: Feedback indicating desirability of transitions or outcomes
questions.wrong1: The target class count in clustering
questions.explanation: Reward signals guide an agent's optimization objective.

questions.text: What makes a Markov decision process Markovian?
questions.correct: The state captures relevant information to predict the next transition given an action
questions.wrong1: The agent remembers every action in history explicitly
questions.explanation: The Markov property conditions future transitions on current state and action.

questions.text: What is an autoencoder commonly trained to do?
questions.correct: Reconstruct its input through a learned representation
questions.explanation: Autoencoders learn compressed or structured representations by reconstruction.

questions.text: Why is an autoencoder's reconstruction error not automatically a calibrated anomaly probability?
questions.correct: Reconstruction loss is not directly a probability of abnormality
questions.wrong1: All reconstruction models use softmax outputs
questions.wrong2: Every anomalous input has zero loss
questions.explanation: Error scores require validation and threshold selection for anomaly detection.

questions.text: What is association-rule support?
questions.correct: Proportion of transactions containing a specified itemset
questions.wrong3: The probability of a class conditional on another class only
questions.explanation: Support measures itemset frequency in transaction data.

questions.text: Why can correlation between two variables fail to establish causation?
questions.correct: Confounders or reverse causality may explain the relationship
questions.wrong2: Causation and correlation are identical by definition
questions.wrong3: A positive correlation always implies intervention success
questions.explanation: Observed association does not alone identify causal effects.

questions.text: What does backpropagation compute?
questions.correct: Gradients of the loss with respect to network parameters
questions.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule through the computation graph.

questions.text: What is the vanishing-gradient problem?
questions.correct: Gradients become very small through deep computation chains
questions.explanation: Small derivatives multiplied over layers can hinder learning.

questions.text: What activation function outputs zero for negative values and its input for positive values?
questions.correct: ReLU
questions.explanation: Rectified linear units compute max(0, x).

questions.text: What is batch normalization primarily intended to do?
questions.correct: Normalize intermediate activations using batch statistics and learned affine parameters
questions.wrong1: Guarantee invariant outputs for every input
questions.explanation: Batch normalization can stabilize optimization and permits learned scaling/offset.

questions.text: What type of network is especially suited to spatial image patterns?
questions.correct: Convolutional neural network
questions.explanation: Convolutions exploit local spatial structure in images.

questions.text: Why can convolutional layers use fewer parameters than fully connected image layers?
questions.correct: Weight sharing reuses filters across spatial locations
questions.wrong2: They require a separate label per pixel
questions.explanation: Shared kernels reduce parameter count while detecting repeated patterns.

questions.text: What does dropout do during training?
questions.correct: Randomly deactivate selected units to regularize learning
questions.wrong1: Delete labeled samples from the disk
questions.explanation: Dropout reduces co-adaptation by randomly masking activations.

questions.text: Why is dropout commonly disabled during inference?
questions.correct: Inference uses deterministic full-network activations with appropriate scaling
questions.wrong1: Inference must always randomly erase all features
questions.explanation: Standard dropout trains with stochastic masks but evaluates deterministically.

questions.text: Which model architecture originally introduced attention as its primary mechanism in 'Attention Is All You Need'?
questions.correct: Transformer
questions.explanation: Transformers use self-attention rather than recurrent connections as the primary sequence mechanism.

questions.text: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide by the square root of key dimension?
questions.correct: It prevents large dot products from pushing softmax into extreme regions
questions.explanation: Scaling moderates variance of attention logits for better optimization.

questions.text: What does an embedding layer do with token identifiers?
questions.correct: Map discrete token IDs to learnable vectors
questions.explanation: An embedding table supplies continuous vectors for discrete symbols.

questions.text: Why is positional information needed by a standard Transformer encoder?
questions.correct: Self-attention alone is permutation-equivariant without position signals
questions.wrong1: Transformers already know absolute order from token ID values
questions.wrong3: Position is encoded in TLS headers
questions.explanation: Position encodings or biases tell the network how tokens are ordered.

questions.text: What is a gradient descent update intended to do?
questions.correct: Change parameters in a direction that reduces loss locally
questions.wrong1: Guarantee the global minimum in one step
questions.explanation: Gradient methods use derivatives to choose parameter updates.

questions.text: Why can a learning rate that is too large prevent convergence?
questions.correct: Updates may overshoot stable low-loss regions
questions.wrong1: Large learning rates always reduce gradients
questions.explanation: Optimization can oscillate or diverge when steps are too aggressive.

questions.text: Which loss is often appropriate for multi-class classification with one correct class?
questions.correct: Categorical cross-entropy
questions.explanation: Cross-entropy measures mismatch between predicted class probabilities and labels.

questions.text: Why are logits often preferred over applying a separate softmax before a cross-entropy loss implementation?
questions.correct: Fused logits-based losses are numerically more stable
questions.wrong1: Logits are already probabilities between 0 and 1
questions.wrong3: Logits remove the need for target labels
questions.explanation: Stable implementations combine log-sum-exp and cross-entropy safely.

questions.text: What is transfer learning?
questions.correct: Adapting a pretrained model to a new task
questions.explanation: Transfer learning reuses representations learned from another dataset.

questions.text: What is catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning?
questions.correct: A model loses previously learned capabilities while adapting to new data
questions.wrong1: A dataset is fully deleted from storage
questions.wrong2: Loss is exactly zero for all batches
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning can overwrite earlier parameter representations.

questions.text: What does a CNN pooling operation typically do?
questions.correct: Reduce spatial resolution by aggregating local regions
questions.wrong1: Add more classes to the dataset
questions.explanation: Pooling summarizes nearby activations and reduces spatial dimensions.

questions.text: Why are residual connections useful in deep networks?
questions.correct: They provide shorter paths for signal and gradient propagation
questions.wrong1: They force every layer's output to zero
questions.explanation: Skip connections make optimization of very deep networks easier.

questions.text: What is the median of 2, 4, 9, 20, 31?
questions.explanation: The median is the middle ordered observation.

questions.text: Why is the median more robust than the mean for extreme outliers?
questions.correct: Extreme values influence ranks less than arithmetic sums
questions.wrong1: The median always uses every numerical difference
questions.wrong2: The mean ignores very large observations
questions.wrong3: Both always move equally under outliers
questions.explanation: The median depends on ordering and is less sensitive to extreme magnitude.

questions.text: What does standard deviation measure?
questions.correct: Spread of observations around the mean
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance.

questions.text: Why is sample variance often divided by n-1?
questions.correct: Bessel's correction adjusts bias when estimating population variance from a sample
questions.explanation: One degree of freedom is used to estimate the sample mean.

questions.text: What does a p-value represent under a null hypothesis?
questions.correct: Probability of data at least as extreme as observed, under the null model
questions.wrong1: Probability that the null hypothesis is true
questions.wrong2: Probability that the alternative is false
questions.wrong3: The size of an observed effect
questions.explanation: P-values condition on a null model rather than assigning probabilities to hypotheses.

questions.text: Why does statistical significance not guarantee practical importance?
questions.correct: A tiny effect can be significant with sufficiently large samples
questions.wrong1: Significant estimates always have large effect sizes
questions.explanation: Effect magnitude and uncertainty must be interpreted separately from p-values.

questions.text: What is a confidence interval designed to report?
questions.correct: A range produced by a procedure with stated long-run coverage
questions.wrong1: The exact probability a fixed parameter lies in one realized interval
questions.wrong2: Always the range of all training observations
questions.wrong3: Only the mode of a distribution
questions.explanation: Frequentist interval procedures have a specified coverage rate across repeated samples.

questions.text: What is the main interpretation of the central limit theorem for sample means?
questions.correct: Under conditions, standardized means approach a normal distribution as sample size grows
questions.wrong2: Every population must already be normally distributed
questions.wrong3: The sample mean always equals the population mean exactly
questions.explanation: The CLT describes sampling distributions under suitable assumptions.

questions.text: Which plot is most appropriate for examining association between two numeric variables?
questions.correct: Scatter plot
questions.explanation: Scatter plots visualize paired quantitative observations.

questions.text: Why should missing values be investigated before imputation?
questions.correct: The missingness mechanism may bias estimates
questions.wrong1: Any imputation always fixes data leakage
questions.wrong3: Deleting all incomplete rows always preserves representativeness
questions.explanation: MCAR, MAR and MNAR mechanisms affect analysis and interpretation.

questions.text: What is one-hot encoding used for?
questions.correct: Convert categorical levels into binary indicator features
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding represents categories with indicator variables.

questions.text: Why can one-hot encoding a high-cardinality identifier be problematic?
questions.correct: It creates many sparse features and may capture spurious identities
questions.wrong3: Identifiers are always continuous numeric targets
questions.explanation: High-cardinality categories can create huge feature spaces and leakage risks.

questions.text: Which statistical measure is bounded between -1 and 1 for linear correlation?
questions.correct: Pearson's r
questions.explanation: Pearson correlation quantifies direction and strength of linear association.

questions.text: Why does a train/test split need to keep records from the same person together in identity-based tasks?
questions.correct: Cross-split identity overlap can leak person-specific features
questions.wrong1: A split changes the number of face pixels
questions.wrong2: Person labels cannot appear in training
questions.wrong3: Test records must always be older than training
questions.explanation: Group-aware splitting measures generalization to unseen individuals.

questions.text: What is an ETL pipeline?
questions.correct: Extract, Transform, Load data into a target system
questions.explanation: ETL processes move and prepare data for analysis.

questions.text: What does a left join preserve in relational data analysis?
questions.correct: All rows from the left table, with nulls for unmatched right rows
questions.wrong1: Only keys present in both tables
questions.wrong2: Only rows in the right table
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN retains the left relation's rows while adding matching right-side data.

questions.text: What is data lineage?
questions.correct: Tracking where data came from and how it was transformed
questions.wrong1: A neural network's number of layers
questions.wrong2: The length of an SQL table name
questions.explanation: Lineage helps audit dataset origins and transformations.

questions.text: Why should a statistical sample be representative of its target population?
questions.correct: Selection bias can make conclusions fail to generalize
questions.wrong1: All large samples are representative automatically
questions.wrong2: Sampling removes the need for uncertainty
questions.explanation: Sampling procedures determine which population conclusions are supported.

questions.text: What is a histogram primarily used to visualize?
questions.correct: Frequency distribution of numeric values across bins
questions.explanation: Histograms group numeric observations into ranges and show counts.

questions.text: Why can an imbalanced dataset benefit from stratified splitting?
questions.correct: It helps preserve target-class proportions across splits
questions.explanation: Stratification reduces the chance of losing rare classes in evaluation partitions.

questions.text: What does precision measure in a binary classifier?
questions.correct: TP / (TP + FP)
questions.explanation: Precision measures the proportion of predicted positives that are correct.

questions.text: Why might maximizing recall be especially important for a medical screening model?
questions.correct: Missing true cases can be costly, depending on deployment consequences
questions.wrong1: Recall counts only correct negative predictions
questions.explanation: Recall measures the share of actual positives detected.

questions.text: What is the F1 score?
questions.correct: Harmonic mean of precision and recall
questions.wrong1: Arithmetic mean of accuracy and loss
questions.explanation: F1 balances precision and recall through their harmonic mean.

questions.text: Why can changing a classification threshold affect precision and recall?
questions.correct: It changes which predicted scores count as positives
questions.wrong2: It retrains all model weights automatically
questions.wrong3: It removes class imbalance from the data
questions.explanation: Threshold selection trades false positives and false negatives.

questions.text: What does a confusion matrix summarize?
questions.correct: Counts of predicted versus actual classes
questions.wrong1: The number of neural network layers
questions.explanation: Confusion matrices display true and false predictions per class.

questions.text: Why may PR-AUC be more informative than accuracy in rare-positive classification?
questions.correct: It focuses on precision and recall over decision thresholds
questions.wrong1: It assumes positive and negative classes are balanced
questions.explanation: Precision-recall curves expose performance on scarce positive classes.

questions.text: What is a model checkpoint?
questions.correct: A saved representation of model state during training
questions.wrong1: The first row of a CSV file
questions.explanation: Checkpoints can preserve learned weights and optimizer state.

questions.text: Why is reproducibility important in machine learning experiments?
questions.correct: Results should be traceable to data, code, seeds and configurations
questions.wrong1: Every experiment should have identical metrics across hardware
questions.explanation: Versioning data and training settings helps reproduce and audit outcomes.

questions.text: What is model drift monitoring?
questions.correct: Detecting changes in data patterns or model behavior after deployment
questions.explanation: Drift checks reveal when deployment conditions differ from training assumptions.

questions.text: How does concept drift differ from covariate shift?
questions.correct: Concept drift changes relationships between features and targets; covariate shift changes feature distribution
questions.wrong1: Both always mean missing data only
questions.wrong3: Covariate shift means target labels are random
questions.explanation: Distribution shifts can affect models in different ways.

questions.text: What does inference latency measure?
questions.correct: Time taken to produce a model prediction
questions.explanation: Inference latency is a performance metric for deployed predictions.

questions.text: Why can a fast model still produce slow application responses?
questions.correct: Database locks, serialization or network overhead may dominate end-to-end latency
questions.wrong1: Fast inference proves every dependency is fast
questions.explanation: End-to-end timing includes processing before and after model inference.

questions.text: What is batching in model inference?
questions.correct: Processing multiple inputs together to improve throughput
questions.explanation: Batching can improve hardware utilization when latency budgets permit.

questions.text: Why can aggressive batching hurt a low-latency monitoring system?
questions.correct: Waiting for a large batch can delay individual alerts
questions.wrong1: Batching always makes each prediction instant
questions.explanation: Throughput optimization can conflict with response-time requirements.

questions.text: What is quantization in neural-network deployment?
questions.correct: Representing weights or activations with lower numerical precision
questions.explanation: Quantization can reduce memory and speed inference with potential accuracy tradeoffs.

questions.text: Why must a quantized detection model be accuracy-tested after conversion?
questions.correct: Lower precision can change predictions and threshold behavior
questions.explanation: Model compression may alter numerical and detection outputs.

questions.text: What is a feature store intended to support?
questions.correct: Consistent management and reuse of model input features
questions.explanation: Feature stores help align feature computation for training and inference.

questions.text: What is shadow deployment of an ML model?
questions.correct: Run a candidate model on live data without using its predictions for decisions
questions.wrong2: Store all predictions only in a browser cookie
questions.explanation: Shadow testing evaluates a candidate safely alongside existing behavior.

questions.text: What does an ROC curve plot?
questions.correct: True positive rate versus false positive rate over thresholds
questions.explanation: ROC visualizes detection and false-alarm tradeoffs.

questions.text: Why does real-world validation need users and environments not seen during training?
questions.correct: Deployment populations and conditions can expose generalization failures
questions.wrong1: A model score is always independent of data domain
questions.wrong2: High training accuracy guarantees deployment reliability
questions.wrong3: User differences never affect vision systems
questions.explanation: Field tests reveal lighting, camera and demographic shifts not captured in training.
